          Premier League Fixture Difficulty: Who Has the Hardest Next Five Games Before the November Break?
        
      
                          
                      Oct 8, 2026
          
                      Oliver Hopkins / Author, Jakob Abrahamson / Design, Ithiel Piñero / Data Viz
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
The Premier League returns this weekend, but some clubs have an easier schedule than others. Who has the toughest and easiest upcoming fixtures? We use the Opta Power Rankings to find out.

With the international break coming to a close, the Premier League returns this weekend. There are five more matchdays before the next pause for international action, giving us a nice, chunky run of games to analyse.
Looking at their prospective fixture lists, though, some teams are going to have a much tougher time of it than others.

We can quantify how difficult each side's next five games are by using the Opta Power Rankings. By taking the average rating, on a global scale of 1-100, of each team’s next five opponents, we can work out who has the hardest and easiest upcoming schedules. On paper, anyway.
Liverpool have the hardest next five games according to the Opta Power Rankings.

Home matches against Manchester City and Arsenal headline their upcoming run, but they also face tough games against high-flying Brentford and Brighton. Those two clubs sit in the top four of the Premier League table as things stand and have shot up the global Power Rankings following their impressive starts.
Brighton are now as high as seventh in the world, with Brentford not far behind in 13th.

Liverpool can’t complain too much. The Reds came into the season with the easiest opening five games, so this is surely the almighty Premier League fixture machine- almost as prescient as the Opta supercomputer, we’ve heard – just evening things out.
Nottingham Forest have the second-hardest set of five fixtures. They, too, face both Arsenal and Manchester City before the next international break.

But first, Oliver Glasner will travel back to his former club Crystal Palace on Matchday 6. He’ll be eyeing that one, along with an away game against Ipswich on MD8, as one of the clearest places to grab points during a difficult spell.

Everyone, including us, is raving about Brighton’s start to the season. They have been one of the league's great entertainers so far, scoring more goals than any other side (16) while also pressing more aggressively than anyone else.
Might the Seagulls be about to have their wings clipped, though?

Brighton have the third-hardest next five matches, including back-to-back games against Liverpool and Manchester City. Then again, plenty of people expected Brighton's Matchday 5 meeting with Arsenal to be their  ‘come back down to earth’ moment, and look how that turned out.

Aston Villa, by contrast, have endured a difficult start to their domestic campaign. They have recorded the fewest shots (48), shots on target (12) and touches in the opposition box (81) so far. Their struggles can be summed up by the fact they have the worst expected goals difference in the division (-4.35).

That was perhaps to be expected given the significant turnover in their squad over the summer. Unai Emery’s team picked up a much-needed victory over Tottenham before the international break, but that remains their only win of the season. Unfortunately, things might not get much easier in the short term. Villa have the fourth-hardest five-game spell coming up of any side.

Leeds United are one of only six teams still unbeaten, but they begin this next stretch with the hardest fixture of the lot: away to Arsenal. Mikel Arteta has won all four of his Premier League meetings with Leeds boss Daniel Farke, his joint-best 100% win rate against any manager he has faced in the top flight.
Leeds’ unbeaten record is going to come under immediate threat, with that trip to Arsenal a major reason why their next five fixtures rank as the fifth-hardest in the competition.
In news that will have Fantasy Premier League managers salivating, Fulham have the mother of all fixture swings when the action resumes.

They face each of the three newly promoted sides across the next three matchdays before taking on Aston Villa and Newcastle. The Cottagers have won seven of their last eight matches against promoted opposition, and this run should provide Álvaro Arbeloa with an excellent opportunity to pick up his first league win as new boss.

Newcastle have made a curious start to the season under new manager Matthias Jaissle. They sit ninth in the Premier League table, but as our analysis earlier in the international break found, that might be a slightly fortuitous position.

D99489F6C2B399745B37CD0CE520F767.title: Preview: Arsenal’s Cup trip to Fleetwood takes them back to Highbury
D99489F6C2B399745B37CD0CE520F767.subtitle: FotMob
paragraphs: NewsAboutTV schedulesPreview: Arsenal’s Cup trip to Fleetwood takes them back to HighburyShareHaving won the Premier League last year, the Gunners will want many more trophies in the coming seasons. Great squad depth often earns clubs a shot at the Carabao Cup and Arsenal are better equipped than most this season.
That should put Arsenal among the front-runners for a semi-final spot at least, even if they keep rotating in the competition, as they surely will do for the trip to Fleetwood Town.

The FA Cup is probably more known for giantkilling than the Carabao Cup, but it certainly can happen – though it would take an extraordinary turnaround in fortunes for that to be the case here. Among the 72 EFL clubs, only six sit below Fleetwood after a dismal start to the new campaign in what is their third season back in League 2, after spending 10 years in League 1. And yet, there’s a case to argue that in the League Cup at least, they’ve already outperformed expectations: this is the first time they have ever played in the fourth round, a club record.

There can be no doubting the rebuild job that Mikel Arteta has done at Arsenal, and ending the long wait for a league title was of paramount importance. But now after signing a new deal, the question becomes whether they will focus on the biggest titles and put everything into that, or whether he wants to be like his old boss: play strong teams everywhere and scoop up trophies of all kinds as regularly as Pep Guardiola did.

Naturally there are differences between the clubs, but the Gunners’ squad is deep, even if they do rotate or add a few young players into these sides. The fact is, he’s approaching the seventh anniversary of his appointment and so far the silverware count stands at two. For the time and amount spent, he needs the next batch to come quicker, closer together.

Fleetwood have won just three of their 13 League Two games so far this term, winning two of six at home. Across all competitions they’ve lost six of the last nine. Arsenal are of course a total contrast, winning every match this term except defeat to Brighton before the international break and drawing at Bayern Munich last week.
Lewis McCann is suspended for the hosts, while Kane Thompson-Sommers is injured. Rhys Bennett is back from a ban.
Bukayo Saka will miss at least six weeks for Arsenal and William Saliba is sidelined too, with Christos Tzolis hoping to make a comeback.

Mikel Merino has something of a reputation now as the guy to win you games off the bench, but he only has one goal (and no assists) this term – which came when he started against Ipswich in an earlier round. Over the last year compared to European elite midfielders, he’s ranked top of 92% of other players for shots, 98% for aerial duels and 100% for goals.
Nothing untoward unless it takes Arsenal a while to take the handbrake off: Fleetwood Town 0-4 Arsenal.

E05488CA0DDFBEC65D6C7C2D7048CC6C.title: Preview: England head to Czechia in the Nations League
E05488CA0DDFBEC65D6C7C2D7048CC6C.subtitle: FotMob
paragraphs: NewsAboutTV schedulesPreview: England head to Czechia in the Nations LeagueShareEngland will be seeking to bounce back from their Nations League defeat to Spain with a trip to Prague to play Czechia.

If England showed two very different faces in their final two matches of the World Cup against Argentina and France, the performance that they put in against Spain erred more towards the latter than the former.

They ended up on the wrong end of a 3-2 home defeat, but there was a point when they would have been 3-1 up had Harry Kane converted his penalty kick early in the second half. But for the second game in a row, the defence looked threadbare, and that’s the biggest clear issue facing Thomas Tuchel.

Meanwhile, about 800 miles west, Czechia were kicking off their campaign with a 2-1 home defeat, losing to goals from the still-not-retired Luka Modrić and Marco Pašalić of Orlando City, with Adam Karabec of Sparta Prague scoring their goal.

This defeat wasn’t especially unexpected, coming off the back of a disappointing World Cup from which they were eliminated at the first stage with one point after drawing with South Africa but losing to South Korea and Mexico. Santi Denia replaced Miroslav Kubek as head coach shortly afterwards.

Czechia have only met each other five times before, with England having won three and Czechia one. Czechia’s win came in qualifying for Euro 2020, when they scored a 2-1 victory in Prague in September 2019. England’s came in June 2021 when they won 1-0 at Wembley in the Covid-delayed finals of the tournament.

As part of the former Czechoslovakia, they can point to a further two wins against England. Indeed, they won the first-ever meeting between them in May 1934, beating them 2-1 in Prague. Their other win came by the same scoreline in 1975 en route to winning the 1976 European Championships. The two were drawn against each other in the World Cup finals, in 1970 and 1982, and England won both, and have seven wins against Czechoslovakia in total.

Neither team will be lining up at full strength for this fixture due to pretournament withdrawals, with Declan Rice, Cole Palmer, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, and Tino Livramento all having withdrawn from the squad before the Spain match. Lewis Hall wasn’t risked against the World Champions after picking up a knock the last weekend before the break for Newcastle, but this was understood to be precautionary and he may now be available for selection. Trent Alexander-Arnold was unused on the bench on Saturday night, but may return, if Tuchel opts to shake up his defence in order to try and tighten it.

But Czechia were hit even harder by withdrawals than England, with David Zima, David Jurasek, Matej Rynes, Tomas Vlcek, Lukas Provod, Denis Visinsky and Tomas Chory all pulling out before the Croatia match, while Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci withdrew on Saturday due to a calf problem and playmaker Ondrej Lingr was left out of the match-day squad for reasons which remain unclear.

Trent Alexander-Arnold has barely played for England over the last two years, with only one substitute’s appearance in their stagnant 1-0 win away to Andorra in June 2025. At 28 years of age, Alexander-Arnold has just 34 England caps, a figure which looks low when you consider that his Real Madrid team-mate Jude Bellingham has 57, and he’s five years younger.

But having been drafted back into the squad, after another poor defensive performance against Spain and seven goals conceded in their last two games, the former Liverpool man may find himself back in the team. He’s only played four games this season for his club side and has only started twice, but his ratings have been decent and that defence really needs some reorganisation.

Vladimír Coufal was a solid presence over the five years that he spent with West Ham United, and he’s still going, both for Hoffenheim in the Bundesliga and for the Czechia national team, and he ranked as their second-best player against Croatia on Saturday night behind goalscorer Adam Karbec.

Their goalkeeping position is also worth watching. There are only two Premier League players in their team, and both of them are goalkeepers. Lukáš Horníček of Newcastle United started the Croatia match, and it’ll be between him, Matěj Kovář of PSV and Antonín Kinský of Spurs to start this time.

England’s last three games have now come against the three other best teams in the world at the moment, and it’s company in which they’ve held their own, despite having lost to two of them. But these three games and the radically different ways in which they’ve played out indicate that Thomas Tuchel might still not be certain of how he wants his England team to play.

There is certainly growing unhappiness at the way in which he’s managing the team. The Argentina set-up was the wrong one, and given that he was pretty much hired to bring a tournament win to England, he might even consider himself slightly fortunate to still be in the position.

But Czechia were poor in the World Cup and they were beaten at home by Croatia in their opening game in the Nations League. There’s little to suggest here that they’ve got enough in the tank to get past England, and they’ve been hit worse by pre-break withdrawals, too. I’ll go for a 3-0 win for England, though such has been the nature of their defence over their last couple of games that I have to admit having some doubts about that ‘nil’.

Add FotMob as a preferred news source on Google by clicking – here.
England will be seeking to bounce back from their Nations League defeat to Spain with a trip to Prague to play Czechia.

If England showed two very different faces in their final two matches of the World Cup against Argentina and France, the performance that they put in against Spain erred more towards the latter than the former.

          UEFA Champions League Top Scorers
        
      
                          
                      Oct 16, 2026
          
                      Matt Furniss / Author, Matt Sisneros / Design
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Which players have scored the most Champions League goals in the history of the competition? Here, we look over the all-time UEFA Champions League top scorers.

Cristiano Ronaldo: 140Lionel Messi: 129Robert Lewandowski: 109Karim Benzema: 90Kylian Mbappé: 72Raúl: 71Erling Haaland: 61Harry Kane: 57Thomas Müller: 57Ruud van Nistelrooy: 56Thierry Henry: 50Mohamed Salah: 50Andriy Shevchenko: 48Zlatan Ibrahimovic: 48Filippo Inzaghi: 46Didier Drogba: 44Antoine Griezmann: 44Neymar: 43Alessandro Del Piero: 42Sergio Agüero: 41
Cristiano Ronaldo is the all-time leading scorer in the UEFA Champions League with 140 goals in 183 appearances.

With the Portuguese now playing at Saudi Arabian club Al Nassr, it’s unlikely that he’ll add to this tally, which he accumulated over spells at Manchester United (21), Real Madrid (105) and Juventus (14).

Ronaldo also holds the record for most goals in a single Champions League season with his 17 goals for Real Madrid in 2013-14, as they won the UCL trophy by beating Atlético Madrid in the final. He followed that up with 16 goals two years later in 2015-16.
The Portuguese legend has won the competition top scorer award on seven different occasions, which is a record across both the European Cup and Champions League eras.
He scored in a record 93 different UCL matches, 51% of his appearances in the competition, while eight of those saw him score a hat-trick, which is a record he shares with Lionel Messi.

Ronaldo found the net against 38 different opponents in his Champions League career, with his 10 goals versus Juventus the most by any single player against an opponent in the history of the competition.

Lionel Messi is the second highest scorer in UEFA Champions League history with 129 goals. He does, however, hold the record of scoring the most goals for a single club in UCL history, with 120 of his 129 goals coming at Barcelona.

He added nine more after moving to Ligue 1 giants Paris Saint-Germain in the summer of 2021, but it's unlikely he'll ever get a chance to add to his goal tally following his move to MLS club Inter Miami.

Messi’s record of scoring against 40 different opponents in the UEFA Champions League is more than anyone else, ahead of Ronaldo on 38. Nine of Messi's goals came against Arsenal (7%), his favourite opponent in the UCL.

Overall, 2022 World Cup winner Messi has scored in 18 different seasons of UCL action, netting in every campaign since 2005-06 after failing to score in his only appearance for Barcelona in his debut campaign of 2004-05. He shares this record with Karim Benzema, but the French striker managed to score in all 18 of the UCL seasons that he played in.

Messi may share the UCL record for the most hat-tricks in the competition with Cristiano Ronaldo (eight), but he once did something the Portuguese never managed: score five goals in a single Champions League match. He managed this in Barcelona’s 7-1 win over Bayer Leverkusen in March 2012 as part of his record-breaking 2011-12 season in which he scored 73 goals in 60 competitive club appearances.
Robert Lewandowski reached his century of UEFA Champions League goals on 26 November, scoring for Barcelona against French club Brest.

Of his 109 UCL goals, 69 came at Bayern Munich after he arrived from Borussia Dortmund. With 23 goals for Barcelona, it means that he was just the second player in Champions League history to score 10+ goals for three different clubs after Cristiano Ronaldo.

He holds Bayern's record for the most goals in Europe, ahead of Gerd Müller (65). He also holds the Bundesliga club’s record for most goals in a single season in this competition, netting 15 times in 2019-20 en route to Bayern lifting the trophy. In doing so, he became the first Polish player to finish as the top scorer in a season of UCL/European Cup action.
His 108th and 109th goals came against Newcastle United in the last 16 of the 2025-26 UCL, meaning he broke the record for the most different opponents scored against in the competition (41).
With his transfer to Al-Ittihad in Saudi Arabia in June 2023, Karim Benzema looks very unlikely to add to his tally of 90 UEFA Champions League goals.
Benzema has scored in the most UCL seasons without having failed to find the net in one, scoring in all 18 seasons of the competition since first appearing in 2005-06 at Lyon.

The French striker won the Champions League top scorer award for the first time ever in 2021-22, with his 15 goals helping Real Madrid to the title, although he failed to score in the final win over Liverpool in Paris.

          Man Utd vs Tottenham Prediction: Premier League Preview
        
      
                          
                      Oct 9, 2026
          
                      Tom Patey / Author
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Both sides need to improve in the Premier League after the international break. Look ahead to Saturday’s clash with our Man Utd vs Tottenham prediction and preview.
A pause for international football allowed Manchester United and Tottenham to assess poor Premier League starts, but they return to action on Saturday when they tussle at Old Trafford.
Spurs have had their worst five-game opening to a Premier League campaign, with two points and a goal difference of -6, eclipsing their 2008-09 struggles (two points, -3 goal difference).

Worryingly for Roberto De Zerbi, more unwanted history could await. Only in 1912-13 (first 12 games), 2008-09 (first eight) and 1955-56 (first six) have Spurs failed to win any of their opening six games of a league campaign.

Tottenham's struggles are are hardly short-term, though. Among ever-present Premier League sides in 2026, they have accumulated the fewest points (18) after only escaping relegation on the final day of last season.
United, meanwhile, have five points from their opening five games, their joint fewest at this stage of a Premier League season (also 5 in 2014-15 under Louis van Gaal).

It could have been worse if not for a late deflected equaliser from Matheus Cunha salvaging a 1-1 draw away to Fulham. They had trailed after Lisandro Martínez’s own goal at Craven Cottage last time out.

The pressure is on Michael Carrick, considering Man Utd are winless across their past three Premier League games (D2 L1), last going four without a win in the competition in May 2025 during an eight-match stretch (D2 L6).

Carrick may suggest the underlying data points to a turnaround being on the horizon. United rank first for shots (113) and fourth for expected goals (9.89 xG) this season, but that does not tell the full story.

United’s 0.08 xG per non-penalty shot is the third-worst average in the competition, suggesting they are largely creating low-value chances. That figure is only better than Nottingham Forest and United's next opponents, Spurs.

Bruno Fernandes has failed to deliver since his hat-trick against Ipswich Town on Matchday 2 – United’s only league win of the season. Carrick will hope goals can come from elsewhere to turn the tide, then.

Indeed, Bryan Mbeumo has been involved in seven goals in his last six Premier League appearances against Tottenham (six goals, one assist). He found the net for United both home and away against them last season.

But Spurs have attacking threats of their own to watch out for. Mohammed Kudus ranks fourth in the competition for take-on success rate (58.8% – 10/17 – 10+ take-ons), despite playing just 123 minutes this campaign.

Kudus also sits second for goal involvements per 90 for Tottenham in the league since the start of last season (0.43 – 900+ mins), but De Zerbi needs more than just the Ghanaian to get his side out of this rut. They at least scored their first two league goals in the 3-2 home defeat to Aston Villa last time out.

Fortunately for De Zerbi, the international break wasn't as unkind to Spurs as it initially appeared. Jan Paul van Hecke and Micky van de Ven are both fit for Sunday despite limping off for the Netherlands, although Pedro Porro, Xavi Simons, Wilson Odobert and Dejan Kulusevski remain absent.

Carrick has some fitness concerns, too. Benjamin Sesko missed the draw with Fulham due to a recurrence of the shin injury that robbed him of a pre-season and he won't be back for Sunday. Noussair Mazraoui is a doubt, while Patrick Dorgu – like Sesko – is definitely out having returned early from international duty; Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Amad Diallo have all been training and could feature, however.
New signing Carlos Baleba is also set to make his United debut having recovered from an ankle injury and trained “a lot” over the past few weeks.

Carrick will no doubt be particularly relieved Mainoo has been able to train and is likely to be available. He leads the Premier League this season for possession won (40), forward pass completion under high pressure (85.7% – 30/35 – 30+ passes) and take-on success (76.9% – 10/13 – 10+ take-ons).
Man Utd were 2-0 winners in this fixture last season, ending a six-game winless run against Spurs in the Premier League.
Goals from Mbeumo and Fernandes did the damage after Cristian Romero’s first-half red card in early February.

Which teams will be relegated from the Premier League this season? Stay up to date with our live Opta supercomputer predictions for the 2026-27 Premier League relegation battle.
The relegation battle in the 2026-27 Premier League could end up being one of the most exciting in recent seasons.

Across the last three Premier League campaigns, only two promoted sides have avoided relegation. Both of those came last season, however, with Leeds United and Sunderland keeping their place in the English top flight.
The trio of promoted clubs have all started relatively well this time around, with Coventry City, Ipswich Town and Hull City impressing across the opening months of the campaign.

Both Fulham and Bournemouth could find themselves in trouble, while Tottenham's performances over recent seasons won't give their fans huge confidence in not being involved in the relegation scrap once again.

E2FA64B895CBB65E1B7875D7D70FDF62.title: Preview: Man City host Brighton for the first of two meetings this week
E2FA64B895CBB65E1B7875D7D70FDF62.subtitle: FotMob
paragraphs: NewsAboutTV schedulesPreview: Man City host Brighton for the first of two meetings this weekShareManchester City will seek to put their underwhelming loss to Aston Villa behind them in the Carabao Cup against Brighton & Hove Albion.

Manchester City’s defeat at Aston Villa on Saturday lunchtime was their second in their last three games, having also lost at home to PSG in the Champions League the week before last. And they now need to bounce back from that with a tricky match in the League Cup against Brighton. It’s a small wobble, following a perfect start to the season.

Brighton & Hove Albion have already knocked Manchester United out of this competition this season, but their excellent start to this season has also taken a tiny knock over the last few days. They were unable to break down the Czech side Jablonec in the Europa Conference League on Thursday night, while on Sunday they went down 2-0 at Liverpool despite putting in an excellent performance at Anfield.

Over the last two seasons, Brighton have had a surprisingly clear upper hand in this fixture. The last two sets of league matches between these two have ended in two wins for Albion and two draws, with Manchester City’s last win coming in April 2024.

The two sides have only ever been drawn to play each other in the League Cup once before and Brighton won that too. The two sides met in the second round of the competition in September 2008, while Brighton were a League One club, and they won the tie on penalty kicks following a 2-2 draw in front of a crowd of 8,700 at their former home, the Withdean Stadium. Different times.
That game took place on the day after City’s transfer of ownership to the Abu Dhabi United group was completed.

The early stages of this competition are often used by managers to give their fringe players a run out, and one player who could feature in this tie is Floyd Samba, who scored twice in City's 5-0 win against Norwich City in the last round. The 17-year-old has also been playing for City’s U19 this season, and played just over an hour of their Champions League win against AEK Athens last week, so should have another opportunity to prove himself here.

Brighton played a strong team in the last round at Old Trafford. With the club now having established themselves in the Premier League, they can now start taking the domestic trophies seriously, and one first-teamer who we may expect to see is Jack Hinshelwood. He’s already missed two months of this season with an injury and has been easing himself back in since earlier this month, and it’s been a successful reintegration. He scored on his return against Kauno Zalgiris in the Europa Conference League and followed that up by scoring again after being introduced as a substitute towards the end of their 5-0 hammering of Crystal Palace.

With both teams competing in Europe this season the schedules are packed, and we can expect to see changes from the teams that played in the Premier League at the weekend. In this respect, Manchester City have far more wiggle room than Brighton. They’re only missing Antoine Semenyo, who’s expected to be out until December with a leg injury.

Brighton, however, have a growing list of casualties. Evan Ferguson, Stefanos Tzimas, Kaoru Mitoma and Femi Azeez will all be absent, but Brighton are also assessing Pascal Struijk, Mats Wieffer, Yakuba Minteh, Zadok Yohanna, Ferdi Kadioglu and Chema Andres before the match. Given the extent of their growing injury list, Fabian Hürzeler may have a tricky time for this match, balancing the players at his disposal with giving some of his players a little rest time.

Silverware is silverware, but given the intensity of the modern game and how stretched the calendar has become, it’s difficult to believe that this particular tie will be at the top of either team’s priority list, especially considering that they’re both back here to do this all again in the Premier League as soon as Saturday afternoon.

Manchester City’s performance at Aston Villa hinted at a team for whom the adrenaline rush of ‘responding to the charges’ may already be wearing off. They’ve won this competition seven times since they last played Brighton in it, a striking reminder of the distorting effect that their alleged bending of the financial rules have had on football in England.

Brighton have something approaching the opposite problem. Formed in 1901, they have yet to win a major trophy in 125 years, and frustration over this has started to bubble a little on the south coast recently, with bitter rivals Crystal Palace having won the FA Cup and the Europa Conference League in the last couple of years. The desire to win a major trophy is starting to become a need.

They’ve had a bit of a wobble in their last couple of matches, but they did play well at Liverpool at the weekend. Their injury position may have a slightly distorting effect on this match, leaving Fabian Hürzeler with little alternative but to play the team at his disposal. They played a strong side at Old Trafford in the last round and got the result, but Hürzeler may have to shuffle, with a busy couple of weeks to come ahead of the international break.

But I’m going to go out on a limb and predict an upset here. 2-1 to Brighton, and Manchester City to be left with just the Premier League, Champions League and FA Cup to concentrate on. Then it’ll all be back here at 3pm the following Saturday to do it all again in the Premier League.

Add FotMob as a preferred news source on Google by clicking – here.
Manchester City will seek to put their underwhelming loss to Aston Villa behind them in the Carabao Cup against Brighton & Hove Albion.

Manchester City’s defeat at Aston Villa on Saturday lunchtime was their second in their last three games, having also lost at home to PSG in the Champions League the week before last. And they now need to bounce back from that with a tricky match in the League Cup against Brighton. It’s a small wobble, following a perfect start to the season.

Brighton & Hove Albion have already knocked Manchester United out of this competition this season, but their excellent start to this season has also taken a tiny knock over the last few days. They were unable to break down the Czech side Jablonec in the Europa Conference League on Thursday night, while on Sunday they went down 2-0 at Liverpool despite putting in an excellent performance at Anfield.

          Have Premier League Corners Been Fixed By the Increased Scrutiny on Grappling?
        
      
                          
                      Oct 2, 2026
          
                      Ali Tweedale / Author, Jakob Abrahamson / Design, Peter McKeever / Data Viz
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Premier League referees have been told to clamp down on holding at corners, and it appears in the numbers as though there has been an immediate impact.

Over the last few years, events in the penalty area at the most common attacking set-piece in football had developed into the kind of a brawl you might be more likely to see in the stands than on the pitch.

And it reached a nadir last season when, at just about every corner, seemingly every player would have their hands all over an opponent. Plenty had no intention of bothering to consider or look at where the ball was.
It all got very ugly as set-pieces became a bigger part of Premier League football than they had arguably ever been before, despite the technical ability of the players reaching a new peak.
Goals flew in in record numbers; 188 were scored from corners in 2025-26, which is the most in any season since the Premier League’s inception.
More goals aren’t necessarily a sign of a problem, of course. It’s generally regarded as a good thing when more goals are scored because that tends to mean we are getting more entertainment.

But the grappling had got so out of control that corners became too difficult to defend. Blocking and holding became so commonplace, so embedded in the tactics of trying to score from a corner, and so natural for the attacking team, that they became too hard to stop.
There were teams that were picking players for their ability in the box. The increase in goals was actually a negative.

And crucially for those in charge of the game, the throng of bodies in the six-yard box and the fact that just about everyone was grappling somebody made it almost impossible to referee properly. Plenty of that undetected holding directly led to a fair few of those goals going in.

So, this summer, Pro Ref, the rebranded name for PGMOL, the body that oversees match officiating in English football, had a rethink. The decision was made that more focus was needed on penalising “holding actions that have clear material impact”. That is, players being prevented from potentially getting to the ball by an opponent who is holding them.

The emphasis was said to be on “non-footballing holding actions that have no place on the football pitch”. Pro Ref attempted to determine precisely what would be deemed a foul, but as with just about all rules in football, the changes were always going to be governed by some degree of subjectivity, meaning there was no chance of preventing the endless debates and scrutiny of every decision.

But the warnings were there from those in charge nonetheless. “We're trying to get the officials to be as confident as they can be to penalise what they see,” said Howard Webb, the Premier League referees’ chief.

“[That means] fewer warnings, more actions penalised, and if there’s any reduction in offences being penalised, it should be a result of a modification of player behaviour rather than us no longer applying it.”
So, what have the first five rounds of Premier League matches in 2026-27 told us about corner-kicks? Have behaviours changed as Webb hoped, and have there been any changes in the output of corners?

The first thing to note is that it certainly appears as though there is less holding. Corners look less messy this season, and although we are only five games into the season, it’s noteworthy that there haven’t been many major flashpoints.

For example, there hasn’t been a single penalty awarded within 25 seconds of a corner this season – for any kind of misdemeanour – when there were 21 last season. That means we have gone from a penalty being awarded at a corner every 18 games last season to none in 50 games so far in 2026-27.

More corners, however, have led to a free-kick being awarded to the defending team. The proportion of corners that have seen a free-kick given within five seconds of the corner being taken this season (3.8%) is, in fact, the highest in any of the seven seasons for which this data is available (since 2020-21 inclusive).

That would imply that the behaviour of defenders has changed for fear of conceding a penalty, while attackers are still trying to get away with it (though it’s not clear to what extent exactly), but are being penalised more for doing so.

The stakes are too high for defenders, but for attackers, potentially conceding a foul when there is a chance of a goal is worth the risk. It may also be the case that defenders are making the most of any contact, knowing that referees are specifically looking out for these fouls.

There has been a penalty awarded for grappling at another kind of set-piece this season. Sunderland were given one in their game against Arsenal following a throw-in, with Ezri Konsa deemed to have fouled Dan Ballard, but the Premier League’s Key Match Incidents panel has since ruled that the penalty was erroneously given.

          England vs Spain Prediction: UEFA Nations League Preview
        
      
                          
                      Sep 24, 2026
          
                      Harry Carr / Author
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Saturday's UEFA Nations League action is headlined by a huge clash at Wembley. We look ahead to the game with our England vs Spain prediction and preview.
Before a stirring semi-final fightback from Argentina, arguably aided by some suspect substitutions from Thomas Tuchel, England were on course to meet Spain in the 2026 FIFA World Cup final.

Instead, following late goals from Enzo Fernández and Lautaro Martínez, the Three Lions had to contest the third-place play-off with France, edging a frantic encounter 6-4, before watching Spain's 1-0 victory over Argentina in the showpiece match from afar.

Having received stern criticism in the wake of that semi-final collapse, Tuchel needs to rebuild some trust with England's fans, and he has a blockbuster fixture to prepare for as Spain visit Wembley Stadium in the UEFA Nations League on Saturday.

England are back in the top tier of the competition after suffering a humiliating relegation to League B in 2022-23, having to fight their way out of the second level in 2024-25. They did so with five wins from six games under interim boss Lee Carsley (L1), with their current three-match winning streak being their longest ever in the competition.

It is important to remember that Tuchel has the best win rate of any England manager to ever lead the team for at least 10 matches, at 77% (P22 W17 D2 L3), while the Three Lions have only averaged more goals per game under Walter Winterbottom (2.8) than Tuchel (2.3).
England have also won 10 of their last 11 competitive home matches (L1), including each of their most recent five without conceding.

Only once in their history have England's men previously won six consecutive competitive home games to nil, under Roy Hodgson and Gareth Southgate between March 2015 and March 2017. That run also spanned Sam Allardyce's short-lived tenure, but he, of course, never got to lead the team out on home soil.

Tuchel has had to contend with a series of withdrawals ahead of this extended, four-game international break, with Tino Livramento, Kobbie Mainoo, Cole Palmer, Marcus Rashford and Declan Rice all pulling out of England's squad.
Everton's James Garner and Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White, neither of whom made the World Cup squad, have been called up as replacements.

Tuchel was criticised for leaving several creative players at home this summer, so Gibbs-White – whose 13 Premier League goals this calendar year are the joint-most alongside Erling Haaland – will hope to seize his opportunity.

But heavy rotation looks unlikely for Saturday's game, at least, which should provide a useful yardstick for the World Cup bronze medallists. Jude Bellingham has scored seven goals in 10 appearances for England in 2026, with David Platt being the last midfielder to net more for them in a calendar year back in 1993 (eight).

He will reprise his partnership with Harry Kane, who is widely seen as a front-runner for the Ballon d'Or. And with one of Kane's main rivals for the award – Barcelona superstar Lamine Yamal – lining up on the other side, that is another storyline to keep an eye on.
Aided by Yamal's brilliance, Spain also reached the final of the 2024-25 Nations League, eventually going down to Portugal on penalties following a 2-2 draw in the final.
Spain's last five Nations League matches have seen them both score 2+ goals and concede 2+ goals, which is the longest run by any nation – in any tier – since the tournament's inception in 2018.

La Roja have reached three of the last four Nations League finals, also losing to France in 2020-21 and beating Croatia on penalties in 2022-23. Excluding spot-kicks, they have lost just one of their last 18 matches in the competition (W10 D7).

And during the last edition of the Nations League, only Cristiano Ronaldo (eight goals) outscored Mikel Oyarzabal (four). The Real Sociedad forward has 26 goal involvements across his last 25 international appearances (19 goals, 7 assists), a run that started with him scoring the winner against England in the Euro 2024 final.

Spain enter the game defending a 38-match unbeaten run in all competitions, winning 29 games and drawing nine in that time. It is the longest ever streak by a European nation, dating back to a 1-0 defeat to Colombia in March 2024, which did take place on English soil, at West Ham United's London Stadium.

Spain's last competitive defeat, which came all the way back in March 2023, also occurred in Britain, as they lost 2-0 to Scotland in a qualifier for Euro 2024. Might that be a positive omen for England?
Spain have won six of their last nine meetings with England across all competitions (D1 L2), most recently winning 2-1 in the Euro 2024 final in Berlin.

paragraphs: BBC HomepageSkip to contentAccessibility HelpYour accountHomeNewsSportEarthReelWorklifeTravelCultureFutureMusicTVWeatherSoundsMore menuMore menuSearch BBCHomeNewsSportEarthReelWorklifeTravelCultureFutureMusicTVWeatherSoundsClose menu BBC SportMenuHomeFootballCricketFormula 1Rugby UTennisGolfCyclingAthleticsMoreA-Z SportsAmerican FootballAthleticsBasketballBoxingCricketCyclingDartsDisability SportFootballFormula 1Gaelic GamesGolfGymnasticsHorse RacingMixed Martial ArtsMotorsportNetballRugby LeagueRugby UnionSnookerSwimmingTennisFull Sports A-ZMore from SportEnglandScotlandWalesNorthern IrelandQuizzesNews FeedsHelp & FAQsAston VillaScores & FixturesTableLive Match UpdatesTop ScorersAsk Me AnythingWho Am I? QuizVilla to sue Carragher over 'unacceptable insults'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jamie Carragher became a pundit following retirement from playing in 2013
Aston Villa say they will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher over what the club branded as "unacceptable insults".
Posting on their social media on Friday, Villa released a statement signed by their chairman Nassef Sawiris accusing Carragher of insulting the Premier League side and its fans.
It added the club would "not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football".
Speaking on the Stick to Football podcast, Carragher attracted criticism from Villa fans by suggesting their manager Unai Emery would be interested in becoming Manchester United's head coach.
Michael Carrick's position at United is hanging in the balance after a dismal start to the campaign and Carragher said "Aston Villa will never be Manchester United".
"Surely he would want that opportunity to manage a giant again," Carragher said.
"There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not.
"So Real Madrid will take Manchester United's best player, they did it with [Cristiano] Ronaldo.
"And there will be teams below Aston Villa, and they'll take their players or manager, so shut the [expletive] up Aston Villa fans. Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."
Carragher, a football pundit for works for Sky Sports and American broadcaster CBS, has already commented on the backlash he received after he told the fans to shut up.
"It was a joke after the stick Villa fans have given me over saying Emery may fancy joining Man Utd," Carragher said on social media.
"I hope these clown clips show me praising Emery/Villa like I have done for years & saying how pleased I was you won [the 2026 Europa League] in Istanbul."
On the Overlap Daily, Carragher went into more detail.

"I just think Unai Emery is the best manager in the league and if you're Man Utd you're thinking 'what's the best we can get?'. I'm not saying he'll go - I'm just saying if it was me I'd ask the question," said Carragher.
"Certain managers are good at certain clubs and that's Emery. He reminds me of Rafa [Benitez]. I think your own ego if someone said 'that's your level' would say 'no I'm not'. That was my point.

"It's grew arms and legs. I ended up telling them to [expletive] which maybe I shouldn't have done but it was all in jest because they've been all over my social timeline. I was saying [expletive] off my socials."

          WSL Match Predictions: The Opta Supercomputer's Picks for This Week
        
      
                          
                      Oct 29, 2026
          
                      Oliver King / Author, Jordan Collins / Design
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
With the help of the Opta supercomputer, we provide our WSL match predictions for Matchday 8 of the 2026-27 season.
There are new leaders in the Women’s Super League heading into MD8, with Chelsea leapfrogging Manchester City to the top of the table last time out.
Just goal difference separates the two sides heading into the next round of fixtures, and Andree Jeglertz's side will be keen to reclaim top spot in their title defence.
But the Citizens come up against fellow high-flyers London City Lionesses, who have Alexia Putellas in their ranks, fresh from claiming her record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.
Chelsea make the short trip across the capital to Charlton Athletic, who are the only side yet to get a point on the board.
In-form Manchester United will be hoping to keep pace with the top three against Everton, with Arsenal and Tottenham looking to do the same against Aston Villa and Birmingham City, respectively.
Brighton take on rivals Crystal Palace, while West Ham welcome Liverpool to the Victoria Road Stadium, but who will come out on top this weekend?
With the help of the Opta supercomputer, we delve into the pre-match insights to find out.
The action begins at Goodison Park in Saturday's only fixture, with Everton and Manchester United doing battle.
Everton were on the end of a 3-2 defeat against Aston Villa last time out, while Elisabeth Terland‘s 89th-minute equaliser helped United to a well-earned 1-1 draw with rivals Manchester City.

The Red Devils have taken 11 points from their opening seven WSL games this season (W3 D2 L2), their lowest ever tally at this stage of a campaign in the competition. However, 10 of those points have come in their last four matches (W3 D1), making them the favourites here.
Eva Olid's side are assigned a 52.2% chance of taking all three points, while Everton's win probability is rated at 24.8%. The likelihood of a draw is 23%.

United's strong position coming into this match owes to their recent record against Everton. They have won six of their seven WSL away games against the Toffees (D1), doing so in each of the last four seasons.
Everton are winless in each of their 14 meetings with United in the WSL (D2 L12) – only West Ham have faced an opponent more times without ever winning in the competition (17 vs Chelsea).
The standout fixture on MD8 comes at the Copperjax Community Stadium on Sunday, with London City Lionesses taking on defending WSL champions Manchester City.

London City have made a strong start after a summer of big spending, with one of those arrivals, former Barcelona captain Putellas, celebrating her third Ballon d'Or crown on Monday, becoming the second woman to do so after former teammate Aitana Bonmati last year.
Putellas has adapted well to life in England, scoring three goals and providing one assist in seven WSL games, but City will present her toughest test since joining London City.
City remain unbeaten in the league this season (W6 D1) and could avoid defeat in each of their opening eight matches of a WSL campaign for the first time since 2018-19 (unbeaten in first 19).

But the two teams are in great form. Only City (16) are currently on a longer winning run at home in the WSL than London City (5), who could become the first ever non-‘big-four' team to win six in a row at home in the competition.

However, it is that kind of opposition that London City have struggled against. They have lost each of their first seven WSL games against the ‘big-four' teams, but have taken four points from their two since, drawing 1-1 with Chelsea and beating Man Utd 2-1.

          Man Utd Are Better Than Results Suggest, But Michael Carrick’s Side Are Having an Identity Crisis 
        
      
                          
                      Oct 8, 2026
          
                      Ryan Benson / Author, Emily Millen / Design
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
After guiding Manchester United to a third-place finish last season, Michael Carrick has overseen a difficult start to 2026-27. Should he be worried?

When Manchester United appointed Michael Carrick on a permanent two-year deal in the summer, for most it seemed like the only logical choice after he’d taken over halfway through the 2025-26 campaign and steered a side who were unspectacular under Ruben Amorim to a third-place finish. It was a just reward for his impact.
But five matches into the 2026-27 Premier League season and the pressure is on.

After winning 12 of his 17 games in charge last season (all in the Premier League), United have won just two of seven in all competitions this term. Those victories came over promoted Ipswich Town and Champions League debutants Sabah.

A 2-0 defeat at promoted Hull City on the opening day of the season was alarming; United then twice let a lead slip at Everton; they (controversially) lost at home to Manchester City despite having a man advantage for over an hour; they let a two-goal lead slip to a far more vibrant Brighton in the EFL Cup, and they could only draw 1-1 at a Fulham side who began Matchday 5 bottom of the table.
Results have been poor. Performances haven’t been much better.

One particularly notable aspect of United’s games this season is how much more of the ball they’ve generally had. Last term under Carrick, United averaged 49.1% possession; in 2026-27, they’ve had 58% in all competitions and that goes up to 59.9% when just looking at the Premier League, so a 22% increase compared to 2025-26.

We are of course talking about a fairly small sample size in 2026-27, including two games against promoted opposition and having a one-man advantage for so long in the derby, so their possession figure could yet come down. Either way, for now it does feel at odds with the strengths associated with Carrick’s squad – namely the quality they have in transition.
For instance, United impressed in the derby before Phil Foden’s red card, but once the onus was on them to take charge following the sending off, they looked uncomfortable.

Their increased time on the ball will also have some impact on their physical metrics, which have been used as a stick to beat them with in the past few weeks due to them covering less distance per 90 (103.1 kilometres) than all but one Premier League club this term. The discourse has often neglected to mention United’s significantly increased time in possession, though, and that their rankings in some top-line running metrics are pretty similar to last term.

So, the very fact United haven’t covered as much ground as other teams doesn’t mean a great deal in isolation. For example, their 9.9 kilometres covered while sprinting this season is slightly more than City (9.7km) and not massively under Brighton’s (10.6km), and they’ve been two of the best teams in the league in 2026-27.
However, there is arguably a link from this to the idea United have issues with intensity.

Most will look to the midfield pairing here, and understandably so. Among the 57 nominal central/defensive midfielders to play at least 90 minutes in the Premier League this term, Youri Tielemans (4.7) and Kobbie Mainoo (4.0) rank 33rd and 39th respectively for out-of-possession sprints per 90 mins. They’re both excellent footballers, and Mainoo’s start to the season has been quite impressive, though mobility and intensity aren’t aspects you’d associate with either.

United’s collective tally of out-of-possession sprints per 90 (89) is a comparable (in fact, slightly higher) figure to what they averaged under Carrick last season (86), however. When they were winning regularly in 2025-26, you’d have done well to find critics making a big deal about a perceived lack of intensity.

If they do have an issue with intensity, then, it’s probably most pertinent in the context of the team’s structure when pressing, or perhaps even their broader pressing strategy, because there has been a shift from last term.

United have proportionately deployed a high block to a greater extent than any other Premier League team this season (42%) and this is up considerably from Carrick’s time in charge last term (26%). For this to be truly effective, it generally requires a team to deploy a high line; this United side looks uneasy playing in such a way because their defence – not too dissimilar to the midfield – lacks mobility.

Their backline can’t be as high as perhaps it should be, meaning there’s more space for the midfield pairing to occupy between attackers pressing high and defenders dropping deep. It’s not that United are then falling into a low block by default, but if the press is played through, gaps can open up quite quickly and it’s not surprising if the midfielders opt to retreat instead of engage.

As the graphic below highlights, only Aston Villa and Brighton (both 38%) have seen a smaller proportion of their pressures come in the middle third of the pitch than United (39%), who’ve also had the second-smallest share of pressures in their own defensive third (25%).

None of this is inherently bad on its own, of course. It all depends on context, and the introduction of Carlos Baleba – who will be fit for his debut after the international break – should give them more ‘oomph’ in the middle. But there’s a strong argument United might not be best suited to utilising a high block; we’ve noted the lack of mobility further down the pitch, but there’s also questions to be asked about how effective their press is.

As outlined, they’ve spent the greatest proportion of time in a high block among Premier League teams this term, and their 4-2-2-2 out-of-possession shape reflects a fairly aggressive man-to-man press. Or at least that’s presumably the intention.

          Océane Hurtré: One of the WSL’s Best-Ever Debut Seasons in the Making?
        
      
                          
                      Oct 21, 2026
          
                      Maya Shah / Author, Jakob Abrahamson / Design
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Océane Hurtré is lighting up the WSL in Birmingham City colours and is already threatening to make history. Are we potentially about to see one of the league's best debut seasons ever?
Birmingham City may be languishing near the foot of the WSL table, but one player has given their campaign a very different complexion.

At just 22, Océane Hurtré has arrived on English football’s biggest domestic stage with the poise of an established star, the speed to unsettle defences and a habit of showing up when her team needs her most. Her September WSL Player of the Month award highlighted just that, and six matches into her WSL career, she is already threatening to make history.

Hurtré's six goals in as many league appearances equalled the most ever scored by a player in their first six WSL games, matching Rachel Williams’ achievement also for Birmingham in 2011. With seven goal involvements already to her name, Hurtré has also surpassed the seasonal totals of all but seven players in Birmingham’s WSL history, and there are plenty of matches remaining.

Only Khadija Shaw (7) has scored more league goals than Hurtré this season. Keeping pace with the league’s most established attacking talent, the winger has emerged as a beacon in a side still finding its feet following promotion.

Hurtré's brace against Crystal Palace was the first by a Birmingham player in the WSL since Louise Quinn in April 2022. Yet it is not simply the volume of her goals that has caught the eye; it is the manner, too.

Last time out against Arsenal, her blistering run and delicate finish over the advancing Misa Rodríguez to give the Blues an unexpected lead encapsulated a player whose greatest asset is her ruthlessness, showing maturity beyond her years when the pressure is at its highest.

That composure transcends club football, too. Hurtré marked her first senior start for France with a goal and an assist, strengthening her case for a place in the squad for the next World Cup should she sustain this form.
All in all, it's been an excellent start to the season for her, but especially in the WSL.
Hurtré’s emergence is all the more striking when set against her first season with Birmingham.

She scored just three goals in WSL 2 last term, accounting for a mere 6.7% of the team’s total. She was also moved around the pitch, however, with only 48% of her minutes coming on the left wing. This season, that figure has risen to 84%, while she has spent the remaining 16% of her minutes on the opposite flank compared to just 4% last term.

Birmingham averaged 58.8% possession in WSL 2 last season; in the top flight, that figure has fallen to 33.3%. Rather than being able to build attacks through long spells on the ball, the Blues have increasingly had to exploit space quickly when possession turns over. Hurtré, with her acceleration and direct running, is ideally suited to that approach.

Against Arsenal, the route to goal was a clear example. Neve Herron threaded a pass through the heart of the Gunners’ defence, allowing Hurtré to burst into the space behind and finish. It was a simple sequence, but one that exposed the danger Birmingham pose when they can turn defence into attack before opponents have time to reset.

The Blues have recorded seven shots from fast breaks this season, with only London City Lionesses (nine) and Manchester City (eight) managing more. Hurtré and Lauren Hemp lead the WSL with four shots apiece following fast breaks, while Hurtré has also registered the joint-most shot-ending carries (11) across Europe’s top five leagues.

More striking still, Hurtré leads the WSL outright for goal-ending carries with four. Across Europe’s top five leagues, only Barcelona’s Claudia Pina matches that total. These are not merely statistics that speak to her speed; they point to a player establishing herself among the world’s most dangerous players.

Among WSL forwards, only Hemp (78) has completed more progressive carries (in-possession movements taking the ball at least five metres upfield) than Hurtré (58), while her average carry distance of 14.6 metres puts her third among forwards, highlighting how she can propel her side up the pitch and out of pressure, a defining feature of her game so far in the top flight.

Her threat is not confined to transition, though. Hurtré has delivered 35 open-play crosses, the second most in the WSL. That breadth of contribution makes her more than a counter-attacking outlet: she can also provide service from wide areas and stretch opposing defences.

For all her ability to carry the ball, it is Hurtré’s finishing that has really grabbed the headlines. She has six goals from 2.68 expected goals (xG), with only Victoria Pelova (+3.39) overperforming in relation to xG by a greater degree in the WSL this season than Hurtré (+3.32).

Such a level of overperformance highlights the standard of Hurtré’s finishing this season, converting chances that would typically be difficult to score from. Unsurprisingly, then, her goals per 90 is through the roof.

The winger's output is especially remarkable given how little time she spends in the penalty area. Hurtré has recorded just 20 touches in the opposition's box, ranking 33rd in the WSL. Yet she has produced more goals than almost anyone in the division, reflecting how clinical she's been.

EFD338AACF4875197F03F27C40E9502F.title: Preview: Barcelona and Real Madrid meet in El Clásico
EFD338AACF4875197F03F27C40E9502F.subtitle: FotMob
paragraphs: NewsAboutTV schedulesPreview: Barcelona and Real Madrid meet in El ClásicoShareBarcelona host Real Madrid as they look to continue their perfect start in LaLiga.
Hansi Flick’s side sit at the top of the table with 27 points from nine games, with the Catalan giants yet to drop a point.
They face a Real Madrid side who are certainly starting to improve, having won each of their last four games in all competitions.
The last time these two sides met was back in May, when Barcelona secured a 2-0 victory thanks to goals from Ferran Torres and Marcus Rashford.
Barcelona have a number of injury problems heading into this game. Dani Olmo, Roony Bardghji, Andreas Christensen, and Eric García have all been ruled out for the home side.
Jules Koundé could also miss out, as he's a doubt due to an ankle injury, with the French international unlikely to be involved.
Rodrygo, Ferland Mendy, and Raúl Asencio have all been ruled out for Real Madrid due to injury. Vinícius Júnior will also be unavailable for the away side as he remains suspended.
The form of Arda Güler and Yan Diomande will certainly lessen the blow for José Mourinho.

In LaLiga, nobody has been able to contain Barcelona's attack or even get close, for that matter. Flick's side have created 33.6 expected goals in their nine matches, scoring a total of 39 goals. To put that into context, that is a whopping 4.3 goals per game.

Barcelona did suffer a defeat in their toughest test of the season so far as they travelled to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League. Despite pulling the game back to 2-2 with just over 10 minutes remaining, PSG secured the victory thanks to goals from Vitinha and Fabián Ruiz to make it 4-2.

Mourinho is certainly getting a tune out of this Madrid side at the moment, but you have to be perfect in order to keep up with Barcelona in LaLiga. Two defeats in the league this season have put them already six points behind Barcelona, despite Mourinho having one of the best points per game records among recent Madrid coaches.

The six-point gap between the two teams is what makes this game so crucial already. A victory for Barcelona will see them have a ridiculous lead for this stage of the season, while a win for Madrid makes things interesting again.

With Vinícius Junior still suspended, there could be a huge chance for Diomande to truly announce himself at Madrid. Barcelona's attacking threat is obvious, so whether Madrid's attack will turn up is the key to this game.

Diomande is on a phenomenal run of form over the last four games, showing he's finally settling in at Madrid. He has six goal contributions in Madrid's last four matches, and he's going to be crucial if they are to secure three points.
It's still difficult to see Barcelona losing. We're going for a 3-1 home win.

          Aston Villa vs Man City Prediction: Premier League Preview
        
      
                          
                      Oct 22, 2026
          
                      Dan Edwards / Author
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
We look ahead to Saturday’s early Premier League kick-off at Villa Park with our Aston Villa vs Man City prediction and preview.

Manchester City are aiming to become just the eighth team in English top-flight history to start a league campaign with eight consecutive wins, but face a stern test against a resurgent Aston Villa side.

Chelsea, who won their first nine games in 2005-06, and Liverpool, who won their first eight games in 2019-20, are the only teams to better City’s start to the current campaign under Enzo Maresca. Both teams went on to lift the title in their respective seasons.

But – separate to all of the goings-on off the field – City are still not regarded as favourites to win the Premier League this season by the Opta supercomputer. Arsenal lead the way with a 47.7% chance of going back-to-back, with City close behind at 39.9% at the time of writing.
While the points have been rolling in, even the clubs’ own fans would admit the performances haven’t been quite as assured as the league table suggests.

According to Opta's expected points table, City are currently the Premier League’s biggest overperformers, with nearly eight points more (21) than expected (13.2) based on the quality of chances for and against in their games.

One-sided defeats against Arsenal in the Community Shield and Paris Saint-Germain in the UEFA Champions League may be more representative of the club’s genuine current level compared to best-in-class opposition.
Could this season bear some similarity to the 2016-17 campaign, when City opened with six straight wins under new manager Pep Guardiola, before ultimately finishing in third place?

Maresca will aim to prove otherwise, but a trip to Villa Park to face an in-form Aston Villa team is represents of his toughest tasks so far as City boss. Villa are better, and have much more quality, than their current position of 12th suggests.

After winning just one of their first five games in all competitions this season as Unai Emery’s dressing room came to grips with losing a handful of their best players, Villa have recovered with five wins from their next six.
Central to their improved performance levels have been summer imports Nicolas Jackson and Johan Manzambi, who have scored eight goals combined in all competitions since the second week of September.

Alas, Manzambi – who has scored or assisted in all three of the games he has started in the Premier League – missed the club’s midweek UEFA Champions League victory against Viking through injury and is considered a doubt for the visit of City.
Should he be deemed fit enough to start, he could become the first Aston Villa player to register a goal or assist in each of their first Premier League starts.

Manzambi is one of a number of injury concerns for Emery. Villa are currently struggling to field a left-back; Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Matteo Ruggeri are both out, while Ian Maatsen may not be fit enough to start.

City aren’t without injury concerns of their own. Erling Haaland hobbled off the pitch against Ipswich last week and was an unused substitute against AEK Athens in midweek. A hat-trick from Phil Foden meant City coped just fine without their leading man, but their ability to do so against Premier League opposition is another question.

As well as having the most goals (8), Haaland has had the most shots (27) and shots on target (13) of any player in the Premier League this season, while he ranks second for big chances (12) and touches in the opposition box (40).
Haaland’s potential absence may be the biggest threat to City’s 100% winning start.
Aston Villa have won four of their last six Premier League games against Manchester City, as many as in their previous 35 against them (D5 L26).
Man City have lost their last two league games against Aston Villa, last losing three in a row to them between August 1962 and September 1966.
Man City made it eight wins from eight games in 43.0% of simulations. The next-most common result was a home victory for Villa, at 31.6%, while the game was drawn in 25.3% of sims.

          Lionel Messi’s Argentina Farewell Match Brings Curtain Down on a Golden Era that Almost Wasn’t
        
      
                          
                      Oct 6, 2026
          
                      Ryan Benson / Author, Jakob Abrahamson / Design
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Lionel Messi will represent Argentina for the last time in a farewell match on Tuesday, closing out a glorious international career that ultimately rewarded his patience.

Not for the first time, Lionel Messi is returning to the Argentina national team. This occasion, however, will be accompanied by a sense of completion and celebration rather than obligation, as the Albiceleste bid farewell to probably the greatest footballer ever.

Messi will don the Argentina shirt one last time in Tuesday’s friendly against Benin (who else?!) after he was invited back for one last celebratory runout following his retirement from international football in the wake of defeat in the 2026 World Cup final.

He did retire once before, of course. In 2016, having suffered heartbreak in a major international final for the third year in a row, adding to the 2007 Copa América runner-up finish, Messi was seemingly done.

“This is tough and a difficult time,” he said after the Copa América Centenario final defeat to Chile. “The first thing that comes to my mind and that I have thought is that the end has come for me and our team. It has been four finals – [international success] just wasn’t for me unfortunately. I looked for it, and wanted it so badly, but it didn’t happen for me.

“I think [international retirement] is best for everyone, firstly for me and for a lot of people that wish this. The team has ended for me, a decision made. I tried many times [to win something with Argentina] and I leave without being able to obtain it.”

Fortunately, about six weeks later following a national campaign urging him to change his mind, Messi confirmed he wasn’t quitting. Another 10 years with the national team would follow, and what a time it ultimately proved to be.

But no, this isn’t another international retirement U-turn. Having finally enjoyed considerable international success, not to mention earning more caps (208 after Tuesday's game) and scoring more goals (125) for Argentina than anyone, Messi no longer has anything to prove to anyone.
Given what we’ve seen Argentina achieve since 2021, the barren spell that coincided with the first 16 years of Messi’s 21-year international career feels like something from an alternate reality.
Copa América final defeats in 2007, 2015 and 2016 were on top of the 1-0 extra-time loss to Germany in the 2014 World Cup decider.
And it wasn’t as if there was a huge amount of promise for Argentina immediately following Messi’s 2016 U-turn.

Debacle is the word that probably best sums up Argentina’s participation at the 2018 World Cup. They were poor in qualifying, reports of a player mutiny stirred relentlessly after a 3-0 loss to Croatia on Matchday 2, and then they were dumped out by France in the round of 16 (admittedly, they did run Les Bleus close in an instant classic in Kazan).

Messi took time away once again after Russia 2018. It was a difficult period for Argentina, who parted ways with Jorge Sampaoli as coach and appointed his assistant in his place. It was a widely unpopular decision that Diego Maradona infamously slammed in his characteristically earnest manner.
“He’s a great guy, but he can't even direct traffic,” Maradona told Clarín. “How can we give the Argentine national team to him? Are we all crazy?”

He was, of course, talking about Lionel Scaloni, who quite plausibly doesn’t know how to direct traffic, and it’s highly likely he never has. But you know what he’s done a pretty good job of directing? The Argentine national team.

Scaloni – and Pablo Aimar – seemingly did enough to convince Messi his absence needn’t be permanent, and what a curious quirk of fate this turned out to be, given Scaloni arguably only got the job because he was an easy and cheap option. Seven years on, he’s the one Argentina coach to win the World Cup and multiple Copa América titles – and it’s fair to say Messi was key to all those successes.
Scaloni is also the Argentina coach Messi has played for the most (79 caps), and that feels symbolic.

Where Scaloni has excelled is in creating a team who maximise Messi’s influence at the top end of the pitch without needing him to muck in off the ball like others, allowing him to focus on what he does best. The rest of the team pick up the slack by working that bit harder, but it’s dirty work that so many of them seem to relish doing, like it’s an honour to do the jobs deemed beneath (or wasted on) Messi.

That might not sound like a particularly kind appraisal of Messi’s teamwork attributes, but it’s hard to argue Scaloni’s recipe didn’t work. And those famous images of the Argentina team walking out to warm up at the 2026 World Cup, looking like Messi was leading his own personal militia, certainly supports the idea they were all in on it.

And why wouldn’t they be? After consecutive Copa América wins either side of glory at Qatar 2022 – their first World Cup triumph since 1986 – and a run to the final at this summer’s World Cup, Argentina have enjoyed the kind of success they’d not seen for generation, maybe longer.
