ftbpro_01m49a4sm0hd.title: ‘Broken His Word’—Cristiano Ronaldo Bares All on Portugal Exit, Jorge Jesus Feud, Retirement Date
ftbpro_01m49a4sm0hd.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Roberto Casillas5:32 PM EDTCristiano Ronaldo held nothing back.   / Maciej Rogowski/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty ImagesAs promised last week, Cristiano Ronaldo has come out with the “absolute truth” of what led to his decision to abandon Portugal’s September-October international camp in a sensational, lengthy and detailed statement that shocked the entire soccer world.

Ronaldo abruptly exited Portugal’s camp last week with two UEFA Nations League games still left to play in the international window, with reports instantly pointing to a rift between the all-time great and Portugal manager Jorge Jesus.

Less than a week later, on the same day that his fierce career rival Lionel Messi bids farewell to Argentina and international soccer, Ronaldo released a nearly 2,000 word statement detailing what led to his Portugal exit, taking aim at Jesus and confirming he isn’t retiring from the Portugal national team.

“This is the truth on what has happened with Jorge Jesus,” Ronaldo’s statement began. “As I promised, I decided to recount, in the first person and directly, the circumstances surrounding the last training camp of the national team.”
What followed was an incredibly detailed account in which Ronaldo touched on a variety of subjects.
FREE NEWSLETTER. New SI FC Newsletter Global Embed. Sign Up to Get Informed With SI FC. dark

“After the 2026 World Cup, I prepared a letter to the Portuguese people, which I still keep, with the words I want to address to them when I leave our team for good. At the end of the competition, already on the flight back from the United States, the President of the Federation (FPF) asked and insisted that I reconsider the decision to leave, because the FPF wanted me to continue.

“Right afterwards he asked me for my opinion on the name of the current head coach, which he was considering alongside other names he did not reveal to me. I told the President of the Federation that, in my opinion, it would be the right choice. That is why, on the day the current head coach was presented, I was genuinely happy with the choice. It was the right option, as the results are confirming.

Jorge Jesus (left) and Cristiano Ronaldo won the 2025–26 Saudi Pro League title at Al Nassr. / Wun Suen/AFP/Getty Images “A few days later I received a first contact from the new national team coach saying he would like to meet me in person. I said yes and we scheduled it for the end of my holidays. We met at the Cidade do Futebol, where my club was holding its preseason training camp. That day the coach told me he was counting on me and that my presence was fundamental to his project. He presented me, right there, with a plan for my participation. He told me I would play the first match and the last one, and that for reasons of physical management he would always make three to four changes per match.

“At that point he raised the possibility of me not traveling with the national team to Norway and Denmark. He proposed that I play the first match and stay in Portugal, then rejoin before the match at the Dragão. I refused this proposal immediately. It seemed obvious to me that I could not accept it. It was not because I would not play the matches abroad that I would stop captaining our team. That privilege of staying in Portugal would not be a good example. The coach ended up agreeing with my point of view.

“This conversation was attended by Simão Coutinho, sporting director of Al Nassr, the person to whom the current head coach reported throughout last season and one of those responsible for his signing by the club in 2025. On the eve of the start of the camp the coach came to my house in Lisbon, at his request, for another conversation with me. The conversation was calm and all the principles agreed in August were maintained. I played the match at Alvalade and, although substituted, I made no problem of it. I put the armband on Bruno Fernandes myself, far from imagining that I might be taking my last steps as a player and captain of the National Team. What mattered to me that day was our victory. Winning is always good; in Portugal and for my country, even better.

Cristiano Ronaldo spent much of the second half warming up but never entered the match against Norway.  / Torbjorn Tande/DeFodi Images/DeFodi/Getty Images “At lunchtime on the day of the match in Norway, an assistant to the head coach came to the table where the group was having lunch and informed me that the head coach wanted to speak to me. To my absolute surprise, the head coach asked me if I was fit to play 30 minutes. I was fully focused on my physical recovery, integrated with my teammates as always, and thinking that I would not play that day. Without any problem. This request was something outside my physical recovery and training plan, because I was only going to play on the 4th [of October] at the Dragão, but I obviously said yes. He replied that I should then be ready because I would play 30 minutes. The rest everyone knows. I warmed up from half-time, watched the minutes go by, and was never called on.
“The head coach had failed to keep his word.

“At the end of the match I only wanted everything to be over with the victory and to be left alone. I did not go to greet the fans. That is a failing that is solely my responsibility and that should not have happened. I apologize to the Portuguese who supported us intensely there, I apologize to the fans, and I apologize to those who, without being Portuguese, may have travelled there to see me and whom I may have disappointed.

“Forty-eight hours later we had a conversation: myself, the head coach and Simão Coutinho, since he had been been present for our conversations in August. It was a deep moment, very frank, without any kind of filter. We agreed that there was only one way to close this ‘issue’: that the head coach repeat what he had just told me in private, in  Simão Coutinho’s presence, but in the press room.

“What was agreed was simple: the head coach would begin the press conference with this subject, seeking to close the matter by telling the truth. He would say that I never asked to play any minutes, that it was the head coach and no one else who proposed the plan for this camp to me, and that it was a mistake to put me on to warm up and then not bring me on, and that if it happened again he would not do it. We ended that meeting with the head coach asking me for a hug, promising me that he would say at the conference what he had just said to me, and that the matter would be put behind us. I would not play in Denmark, and I would play the match at the Dragão. All of this in the presence of Simão Coutinho, always.

“At the head coach’s request, a meeting then took place between himself, Simão Coutinho and Tiago Craveiro by video conference, in which what we had discussed was summarized. A short document was produced which I myself validated and which, with my knowledge, was delivered to the head coach, as he had requested. The conference was what is known: the posture had nothing to do with our meeting; I heard expressions and an aggressiveness that I do not believe I deserved, a ‘high and mighty’ attitude that he never showed me, not even remotely, in private the day before.

Jorge Jesus deviated from the script in a now infamous press conference, per Ronaldo.  / Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/NurPhoto/Getty Images “The notes I validated [for Jesus to deliver] were as follows:

“I think it is important, also because it is the truth, to clarify a few things before talking about Denmark:1.  I myself, and no one else, proposed a plan to Cristiano for this season with the national team. It was a long and very good conversation.2.  I know how much he lives for and loves the national team and the weight he has in the world, and even more the weight and the positive influence he has had on the national team for 24 consecutive years.3.  The plan I proposed to Cristiano was accepted.4.  He never questioned my choices. He was exemplary, loyal and professional.5.  The match in Norway was not part of the plan I drew up for him. However, I felt that he had managed to recover physically from the first match, and I warned him that I might have to use him. Cristiano agreed.6.  I made a mistake in having someone of the stature of Pelé or Maradona warm up and then not putting him in the game. If it were today I would not do it.7.  To close the matter: I want Cristiano in the national team. In fact I don’t want him a little, I want him a lot. Fortunately he also believes in me. He believed at Al Nassr and he does here too.8.  On not having greeted the fans. We have already talked about that. Someone who has played more than 230 matches for the national team does not receive lessons from me on love for Portugal. It was a moment of frustration that erases nothing. He is the player who gives the most autographs, takes the most selfies, and shows the most affection to the fans. Let us not invent problems where they do not exist. When we are not happy, we react. That was all.
“None of these notes, therefore, required the head coach to even apologize to me. It was the second time he was failing to keep his word with me.

ftbpro_01m49fczgk8y.title: Mauricio Pochettino Identifies Biggest Threat to USMNT in Match vs. Canada
ftbpro_01m49fczgk8y.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Sophia Vesely6:08 PM EDTThe USMNT is seeking a fourth-consecutive victory. /  Omar Vega/Getty ImagesThere is one thing standing in the way of the U.S. men’s national team and a perfect record this fall: Canada, and to be more specific, Jonathan David.

After three-consecutive victories this fall, including the weekend’s emphatic 3–0 result against bitter rival Mexico, the USMNT is flying high in the dawn of its new youthful era. The Stars and Stripes will look to make it a perfect four for four to conclude the fall international window when they clash with their neighbors to the north, another major Concacaf foe.

Tuesday night’s match at Allianz Field harbors one major threat in particular, according to USMNT manager Mauricio Pochettino, a “fantastic striker” for Canada that has the means of denying his team glory.
“There is a good mix in his qualities,” Pochettino said about David pre-match. “Scoring goals with confidence, he is going to be a difficult player for us tomorrow.”

The 26-year-old has been at the scene of the crime before, preventing Pochettino from defeating Les Rouges on more than one occasion. In fact, Pochettino has never reigned victorious over Canada since taking over in 2024.
FREE NEWSLETTER. New SI FC Newsletter Global Embed. Sign Up to Get Informed With SI FC. dark

David has bested the USMNT in the last two match-ups. /  Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesPochettino has long been familiar with David’s game. As the former manager of Tottenham Hotspur, Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea, the Argentine boss admits he always had his sights set on the talented striker, who starred for Lille between 2020–25.

“I know the type of player that he is,” Pochettino said about the current Atlético Madrid star, on a season-loan from Juventus. “We were always in different clubs. He was always on our radar to try to sign him. That is the truth.
“And now, seeing him in La Liga, in a club like Atlético Madrid, with a coach like Diego Simeone, it is fantastic.”

Since taking over for the Stars and Stripes, Pochettino has regrettably become even more familiarized with David’s dominance. The USMNT has lost its last two clashes with Canada, both 2–1 results, in September 2024 and March 2025. In both matches, David scored the game-winner; the most recent one was a 59th-minute left-footed blast to condemn the USMNT to an abysmal fourth place in Concacaf Nations League.
“We need to be focused on him, of course, because he is one of the greatest strikers today in the world,” Pochettino added. “Not only here and in Europe, but the world.”

The 2024–25 Concacaf Men’s Player of the Year has 43 goals for Canada in 84 international appearances, making him the nation’s all-time leading scorer. He is currently enjoying a strong run of form with Atléti, scoring in the last three club matches.
Anticipated to lead the line for Canada on Tuesday night, it will most likely be USMNT star center back Chris Richards’s job to contain him. Pochettino will hope he is up for the task.

ftbpro_01m49k2j6y5x.title: After Making USMNT History, Diego Kochen Eyes Return to European Giants
ftbpro_01m49k2j6y5x.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Roberto Casillas7:15 AM EDTDiego Kochen could be the USMNT’s goalkeeper of the future.     / Rich Storry/Getty Images Fresh off making U.S. men’s national team history, Diego Kochen admitted that one day returning to boyhood club Barcelona to become the club’s top-choice goalkeeper is “one of my goals.”

The youngest goalkeeper to ever start a game for the USMNT against Mexico left Barcelona on loan this summer, joining newly-promoted side Lyngby in Denmark’s top flight. A relatively cheap buy option was included in the deal and the Catalans kept a sell-on clause reportedly in the neighborhood of 40%. Kocken, though, didn’t hide his desire of one day returning to the Spanish giants.
“I obviously have my long-term goals,” Kochen told GOAL. “I’m on loan right now with Lyngby, so one of my goals is to compete as much as possible and give everything I have for that club.
“At the same time, I come from Barcelona, so to be able to go back? It’d be any kid’s dream to go back to such a big club and have the opportunity there. That's another one of my goals.”
The Florida native has big ambitions, but can you really blame him? He’s spent seven years with the Catalans and was tantalizingly close to making his official debut with the club.
Sign Up to Get Informed With SI FC. dark. FREE NEWSLETTER. New SI FC Newsletter Global Embed

Diego Kochen was a regular in Barcelona’s matchday squads in 2025–“6.  / Angel Martinez/Getty Images Kochen joined Barcelona’s famous La Masia upon arriving in Catalonia in 2019 when he was only 13. The goalkeeper has since progressed through the club’s academy ranks, sharing the pitch with young up-and-coming players such as Marc Guiu and Héctor Fort.
Eventually he became a regular for Barcelona‘s B team, training under current Mexico manager Rafael Márquez and sharing the pitch with the likes of Lamine Yamal, Pau Cubarsí and Marc Bernal.

Last season, Hansi Flick trusted the young American and made him the third-choice goalkeeper following the departure of Marc-André ter Stegen. When starter Joan García suffered a knee injury early in 2025–26, The Athletic reported Kochen was very close to making his maiden La Liga start for Barça given backup Wojciech Szczęsny was dealing with fitness issues himself.

Kocehn’s official debut wasn’t to be, but he did play for Barça’s senior side in a friendly against Club América in Dec. 2023. He remains a highly regarded prospect in Catalonia, but at 20, with no path to consistent playing time, leaving the club to get regular minutes was essential for his development.

Kochen became Lyngby starter immediately upon arrival, which led to him being included in Mauricio Pochettino’s USMNT roster for the September-October international action. Against Peru, he made his debut. Then came a history-making showing.

Diego Kochen made his first USMNT start against Mexico.  / Kevin Abele/Icon Sportswire/Getty Images Kochen became the youngest player in USMNT history to start against arch-rival Mexico. Overall, it couldn’t have gone much better for the Barcelona loanee, as he kept a clean sheet and the Stars and Stripes demolished El Tri 3–0.

“It’s such an honor to represent this country,” Kochen told Telemundo after the match. “In such a big stadium and against this rival—who are our rival. I’m very thankful to the team, the staff and the manager for trustuing me,” he added.

It hasn’t taken long for some of his USMNT teammates to notice his Barcelona upbringing. “He’s come through the Barcelona academy, so I know that he's definitely good with his feet,” center back Chris Richards said.
Kochen is slowly finding his footing both at the senior club and international level. If he continues his recent surge, he’s got a very good chance of becoming the USMNT’s starter of the 2030 cycle.
And who’s to say that his dream return to Barcelona doesn’t materialize in the future?

ftbpro_01m49sef6dqc.title: USMNT Player Ratings vs. Canada: American Boys See Out Perfect Fall Window
ftbpro_01m49sef6dqc.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Sophia VeselyOct 6, 2026Justin Ellis (right) had the game winner on Tuesday. / Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty ImagesThe U.S. men’s national team saw out a perfect fall, winning its fourth-consecutive match on Tuesday night with a 1–0 result against Canada.

The affair at Allianz Field in St. Paul—although not as goal-frenzied as the previous wins against Peru, Chile and Mexico—nonetheless proved the Stars and Stripes’ steady dominance and their incredibly bright future.
It also marked the USMNT’s first win against Canada since 2024 and of manager Mauricio Pochettino’s tenure.

The Argentine boss will be incredibly pleased with how his team prevailed over the past two weeks and the contributions his several newcomers made, including 19-year-old Justin Ellis’s game-winner in the first half.
dark. FREE NEWSLETTER. New SI FC Newsletter Global Embed. Sign Up to Get Informed With SI FC

Justin Ellis (right) had the game winner on Tuesday. /  Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty ImagesIt was a look of relief, rather than excitement, on Ellis’s face upon scoring in the 29th minute, a goal that would prove to be the game-winner.

The young striker was no doubt in agonizing pain in that moment, having suffered a major ankle injury less than 10 minutes prior, thanks to a swift kick to the leg from Canadian midfielder Stephen Eustaquio.

Upon that tackle, Ellis fell immediately to the pitch, curled up, clutching his lower leg. After medical assistance, Ellis was able to stand up by himself, but he had an intense limp. Nevertheless, he refused to leave the pitch. He was on a mission to find the back of the net, no matter how much it hurt.

So when the opportunity arose just seven minutes later, the teenager wasn’t going to waste it. He didn’t know how much more his ankle had left to give. Sprinting (or rather, hobbling) into Canada’s penalty box, he met a pinpointed cross from fullback Alex Freeman. Ellis threw his leg out frantically, redirecting the ball into the back of the net.
Pochettino will not soon forget the grit and determination that Ellis showed throughout the first half, and that play alone may have solidified him another call-up in November.
Alex Freeman was brilliant on Tuesday night. /  David Berding/USSF/Getty Images*Ratings provided by FotMob*
GK: Brian Schwake—7.3: Solid display in his first-career start, but wasn’t incredibly tested.

RB: Alex Freeman—8.4: Shut winger Liam Millar down effectively in the corner with strong one-vs.-one defending. His keen vision regarding when to make dangerous runs into the final third—and the foot skills he often employs to do so—continues to set him apart. Had a brilliant assist for Ellis.
CB: Chris Richards—6.8: Effective in gradually pushing up the backline in possession to put Canada on its back heels.
CB: George Campbell—6.8: Had a big clearance from the penalty box in the 23rd minute after a moment of carelessness from partner Richards. Almost had an own goal in the 67th minute.

LB: Auston Trusty—6.7: Performed better at center back than left back this fall. Nonetheless, his ability to do both could make him indispensable for Pochettino moving forward. Trusty is also confident taking control of the air on defensive set-pieces.

CM: Brooklyn Raines—6.9: Looked much more at ease in the midfield than he did against Chile and carved out a discernible role for himself as distributor and ball-winner. He also pulled some silky moves, much to the Canada defenders’ dismay.
CM: Yunus Musah—6.1: Had a few bursts of dynamic movement, but mostly looked slow and stiff.

RW: Giovanni Reyna—6.9: Only player to start all four matches this window. Quickly establishing himself as Pochettino’s right-hand man. Could be a consistent starter in Concacaf Nations League play next month.

AM: Malik Tillman—7.2: He was everywhere throughout the central zone of the field. His ability to get involved in every facet of the midfield as well as on the front line makes him the creative heartbeat of the attack.

ftbpro_01m49tx735ss.title: Three Takeaways From USMNT’s Victory Over Canada That Sealed Perfection
ftbpro_01m49tx735ss.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Roberto Casillas, Sophia Vesely12:04 AM EDTJustin Ellis scored the game’s only goal. / Omar Vega/Getty ImagesThe U.S. men’s national team cruised to a 1–0 win over Concacaf foe Canada on Tuesday night, marking its fourth-consecutive victory to close out the September-October international window in utter perfection.

The Stars and Stripes have yet to experience anything other than victory since the end of the 2026 World Cup this summer, suggesting manager Mauricio Pochettino’s bid for a dramatic program refresh is already paying off.

Although there are several broader points to consider from the team’s two-week international camp (which Sports Illustrated will explore elsewhere), Tuesday’s affair at Allianz Field alone was quite illuminating.
Here are the three takeaways from the clash in St. Paul.
FREE NEWSLETTER. New SI FC Newsletter Global Embed. Sign Up to Get Informed With SI FC. dark

Giovanni Reyna has earned Mauricio Pochettino’s full trust.  / Chris Coduto/Getty Images Tuesday’s match marked a fourth-consecutive appearance for Giovanni Reyna in the starting lineup. He was the only player to start every match of the September-October international window, in an extreme return to the team’s good graces

A former wonderkid back in 2020, Reyna soon became better known for his off-field controversies, quick falling completely out of rotation with the national team. He snuck his way back into the player pool just last year, thanks to Pochettino’s unique appreciation for his playing style; however, he was still nothing more than a bench reinforcement for the majority of the 2026 World Cup.

Now, though, it appears he has fully won over Pochettino’s trust, playing free and flashing the quality that had many once claiming he was a generational talent. He was the most active and dynamic midfielder on the pitch against Canada, critically important for getting his teammates in dangerous attacking spaces.
Next. Gio Reyna Feature on Family Drama. Once at the Center of USMNT Drama, Gio Reyna Is Writing a Different Story. dark

Starting four games in a row might seem like a small feat, but it was a telling one this fall, considering how committed Pochettino was to heavily rotating and fully trialing each of his 12 newcomers. It was also a massive deal for Reyna specifically. Last season, injuries and poor form saw him make just four total Bundesliga starts for Borussia Mönchengladbach. He needs opportunities like these to prove he can handle bigger responsibilities and extended periods of time on the pitch.

Reyna moved to Ligue 1 side Strasbourg this summer and has now started eight-consecutive games for club and country. He’s producing too, scoring a goal for Strasbourg last month and bagging two assists in the opening two games of the international window. He was also at the heart of the USMNT’s opener against Mexico.

The difference-making quality has always been there, but consistency has been Reyna’s main enemy over the years. Now, the 23-year-old is enjoying himself, and Pochettino is keen to finally help the talented playmaker reach his sky-high potential.

Justin Ellis (left) was back among the goals.  / Omar Vega/Getty Images 19-year-old Justin Ellis scored Tuesday’s lone goal, crashing the net in the 29th minute off of a darted cross from fullback Alex Freeman. It solidified a theme that has been building up over the past few weeks: Dang, these kids are good.
Pochettino imparted a lot of trust on his youngsters like Ellis, who were experiencing their very first senior camp, and they repaid himself massively, playing key roles in all four wins.

Ellis’s game winner wasn’t even the first goal he scored this window. Just four minutes into his debut against Peru, he found the back of the net with a header. In total, seven of the 12 goals scored over the past four matches came from teenagers. The American kids are carrying their weight and have turned the USMNT into a goal-scoring machine.

Mauricio Pochettino (left) finally got his first win against Jesse Marsch’s Canada.  / Omar Vega/Getty Images The 2030 World Cup cycle has been ignited perfectly for the USMNT, who not only collected its fourth-straight win but has now defeated both of its most bitter rivals, Canada and Mexico. It signified the first time Pochettino has bested either team since taking over the Stars and Stripes in 2024.

The USMNT didn’t just win either. It completely outplayed its regional foes, doing so with 12 debutants on the roster and devoid of some of the team’s most seasoned players in Weston McKennie, Folarin Balogun and Christian Pulisic. On Tuesday, the Americans slowly but surely wore down Canada and always appeared the side most in control. Mexico was simply embarrassed.

Ahead of the fall camp, Pochettino’s main ambition wasn’t even winning. The window consisted of four international friendlies, after all. That mindset extended into Tuesday, seeing the manager heavily rotate the side he employed against Mexico. The Argentine boss has been chiefly focused on development, experimenting with new players and his roster for the future.
Nevertheless, the team has found a way to win, time and time again, which only begs the question: How unstoppable will the USMNT be when winning is actually at the forefront of the mind?

ftbpro_01m49z5586rw.title: Lionel Messi Bids Farewell to Argentina in Poetic, Emotional, Fairytale Last Dance
ftbpro_01m49z5586rw.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Roberto CasillasOct 6, 2026Lionel Messi’s final Argentina match was a worthy send-off for the greatest of all time.  / Marcelo Endelli/Getty Images (Drone show), Juan Mabromata/AFP/Getty Images (Messi and his kids), Luis Robayo/AFP/Getty Images (Messi, Messi touching chest), Tobias Skarlovnik/Getty Images (Messi drum)In an incredibly emotional night, Lionel Messi played his final game with the Argentina national team. After more than 20 years donning the Albiceleste, Messi closed the book on his international career and Argentina’s most successful era.
“I promise you that if it was up to me I’d be here my entire life. Because playing for Argentina is the most beautiful thing that can happen to anyone.”
Argentina defeated Benin 3–0 on Tuesday night in Lionel Messi’s final appearance with La Albiceleste, with him assisting the first two and then scoring the third.
What transpired during the 90 minutes was as expected. The night as a whole, though, was nothing short of a fairytale.
Sign Up to Get Informed With SI FC. dark. FREE NEWSLETTER. New SI FC Newsletter Global Embed

Lionel Messi scored in his last ever appearance for Argentina.  / Getty ImagesBenin ended up being a much more capable foe than originally thought, perhaps because the African side went against its public game-plan and decided to mark Messi after all. But after a relatively quiet first half in which Messi was still wiping tears, Argentina took over the final 45 minutes.

La Albiceleste opened the scoring in poetic fashion. Messi floated a corner that was volleyed home by none other than the longest-serving teammate of his international career: Nicolás Otamendi. On a night where the legendary center back also bid farewell to La Albiceleste, his final kick of the ball was a goal assisted by Messi.

Then came the passing of the torch. Argentina’s second of the night was also assisted by Messi, but it was a simply wonderful curling strike from the player many expect to become his heir: Nico Paz. The 22-year-old attacking midfielder scored a goal straight out of Messi’s catalogue, highlighting why may consider him Argentina’s next great No. 10.

But Messi needed his goal, and when Agustín Giay was taken down inside the penalty area, the whole world knew what was coming. Messi stepped up and fired a powerful shot into the top corner to score his 126th and final goal for Argentina.

Three memorable goal involvements in his last Argentina appearance that will be remembered forever. And, if it wasn’t enough, he also created the most chances (four), had the most touches in the opposition’s box (12) and the most shots (nine).

Lionel Messi could barely keep it together when he delivered his final speech as Argentina’s captain.   / Juan Mabromata/AFP/Getty Images What he produced on the pitch was characteristically sensational. But once the final whistle blew, the entire Monumental braced itself for Messi’s farewell speech. After a drone show depicting Messi’s best moments with Argentina illuminated the night sky and a special musical performance, Messi took the microphone and addressed an entire nation.

“It’s difficult to say something today,” Messi started. “There’s too many emotions, a lot of things crossing my mind. The first thing I think about is my father. There’s nothing for me to do but say ‘Thank you,’ as I said in my retirement letter.

“It was a massive honor to defend this shirt for more than 20 years. Even during the worst moments we went through, I never stopped fighting, of giving it my all and being here always. Not coming here anymore will be very painful. I  promise you that if it was up to me, I’d be here my entire life. Because playing for Argentina is the most beautiful thing that can happen to anyone.
“Even though I wish I could stay here for the rest of my life, I feel like this is the moment.”
Messi went on to speak on the toll the 2026 World Cup took on him, while also rejecting any conspiracy theories of the team’s poor performance in the final against Spain.

Messi continued: “I want to thank my teammates for the time I shared with this group. They made me fulfill a childhood dream, winning the World Cup, the Copa América, the Finalissima, champions of everything we played for.”
“I’m going to miss playing here so much,” he added. “I had the luck to go all over the country, and I always received so much love. I’m very thankful for what I got to live.”

Lionel Messi was in tear at various points of the night.  / Luis Robayo/AFP/Getty Images Tears streamed down Messi’s face on the way to the stadium, during the national anthem, during the drone show and then in his speech. He wasn’t alone, Lionel Scaloni cried during the anthem, and thousands in attendance were sobbing once the game ended. As Messi continued speaking, Franco Mastantuono, Enzo Fernández, Cristian Romero where among the sobbing Argentina players.

“Today, here again, I surely it’s time for me to live the saddest day of my career,” Messi said after remembering the celebration after the 2022 World Cup at the Monumental. “Because it’s when I say goodbye to the national team and all of you.”
“I’m going to miss defending the colors of the national team, but now I’m going to be on that side, with all of you, supporting these guys in whatever comes. Always together.”

ftbpro_01m4apy21d7k.title: ‘The Reality Is’—Messi Addresses World Cup Conspiracy Theory on Argentina Farewell
ftbpro_01m4apy21d7k.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Grey Whitebloom9:15 AM EDTThe moment got the better of Lionel Messi. / Luis ROBAYO/AFP/Getty ImagesIn 2016, Diego Maradona, Argentina’s greatest player before another left-footed trickster came alone, was caught on a hot mic talking to his Brazilian counterpart Pelé about Lionel Messi.
“Yes, he’s a good person, but he lacks personality,” Maradona shrugged. “He doesn’t have the personality to be a leader.”

A few weeks later, Messi would retire from the national team in tears and without a major trophy to his name. A decade later, it was another emotional farewell, but by now, the shy boy who would quake in Maradona’s shadow had grown into a leader the entire nation was willing to follow off the edge of a cliff.
Messi took the microphone and didn’t want to let go, covering a wealth of topics in an emotional farewell speech which marked the end of an era and the completion of his international transformation.
Feature. Messi Argentina Farewell Feature. How Lionel Messi Rewrote His Argentina Story. dark

Lionel Messi has ended his last two Argentina games in tears. / Paul ELLIS/AFP/Getty ImagesArgentina’s run to this summer’s World Cup final was chaotic, toxic and controversial. Opponents railed against certain refereeing decisions which went the way of the defending champion, while some in South America concocted a theory that the title was denied through nefarious means.

“Let’s be calm guys. Let’s just think about playing,” Messi was caught telling his compatriots in the tunnel before the World Cup final against Spain. “Let’s forget about everything, O.K.? Let’s just think about playing, people, come on.”
Scaloni dismissed the faint whiff of scandal out of hand at the time and Messi was keen to stress that the justification for Argentina’s listless display was as simple as fatigue.

“We dreamed of becoming world champions again; we came so close, and the reality is that nothing strange happened,” he insisted from the middle of River Plate’s pitch at the Monumental. “We gave it our all; the match against England took a huge toll on us, both physically and emotionally. The reality is that we were running on fumes.
“We fought as we always have—as we always did in this jersey—alongside all the teammates I shared the pitch with. Rest assured that every teammate by my side always gave everything for this jersey.”

It felt fitting that Nico Paz should score on Messi’s farewell. / Luis ROBAYO/AFP/Getty ImagesThis was a night to look back and forward—unfortunately for Benin, barely anyone was focused on the present match. Yet, when Messi turned his attention to what awaited Argentina in his absence, he wasn’t entirely optimistic.
“Tough times will surely come,” he warned, “because what we achieved over this period isn’t the norm.”
Any team is going to suffer when the heartbeat of the side is ripped out, as Argentina has proven in years gone by.

Between 1986 and 1993, an Argentina team spearheaded by Diego Maradona won the World Cup and two Copas América, while also finishing second on the global stage. It was seven years of success at the major tournaments—what went on between was rarely so impressive—but it would take 11 years for the country to even make it past the quarterfinals after that golden run.

Messi was made an honorary member of River Plate before Tuesday’s farewell at the Buenos Aires club’s stadium. More than 25 years earlier, River had overlooked Messi even after he scored 12 goals in his trial. That decision would force the diminutive teenager abroad but two of his most memorable moments in Argentina’s kit would bring him back to the Monumental.

“It was here that I experienced one of the happiest days of my career: when we played again after winning the World Cup,” Messi revealed. “I will never forget what I experienced that day. It was beautiful. Even now, when I watch videos of it, I get emotional. That day will go down in history—for me, for all of them, and for my family... It was spectacular; thank you so much.
“Today, being back here, I am likely facing the saddest day of my career, because this is where I say goodbye to the national team and to all of you.

Now that he is no longer a player, Messi will take on the role of a fan. “I will miss defending the national team’s colors, but now I’ll be on the other side—right there with you all—backing these guys and whatever comes next,” he smiled. “Always united.”
The loyal base Messi will be joining earned their own gushing praise from the departing captain. “I was lucky enough to travel across the country and always received so much love,” he beamed.

ftbpro_01m4asgscnx3.title: What Next for Cristiano Ronaldo, Portugal After Wild Statement
ftbpro_01m4asgscnx3.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By James Cormack5:30 PM EDTCristiano Ronaldo’s ridiculously long statement has hardly salvaged the situation. / Jose Manuel Alvarez Rey/Getty ImagesJorge Jesus is minutes into his press conference ahead of Portugal’s Nations League duel with Denmark.

The 72-year-old squirms in his chair as the self-respect he’s developed over a coaching career spanning 36 years, during which he collected titles on three continents, seeps out of him with each gushing word. He’s begrudgingly maneuvered through five of the pre-arranged points to get across to the group of journalists in front, manifesting as a pack of hyenas. They smell weakness.

And then comes the killer blow. Jesus clears his throat and unleashes: "I made a mistake by putting someone of the stature of Pelé or [Diego] Maradona on to warm up and then not putting him in the game. If it were today I would not do it."
That’s it; he’s cleared the point of no return. He’s at the mercy of a 41-year-old man-child desperate to save face after an embarrassing ordeal.

Of course, the aforementioned affair merely occurred in the increasingly fantastical world of Cristiano Ronaldo. The public resolution he sought from Jesus never arrived—the manager’s second broken promise—sparking his withdrawal from the Portuguese camp.

The sequence of events, culminating in a near-2,000-word statement that only Piers Morgan would endorse, has ignited serious doubt over Ronaldo’s future with the national team. While his great contemporary rival, Lionel Messi, has just celebrated the most dignified of farewells, Ronaldo is seemingly bowing out of the international stage on very different terms.
We’re not going to run you through a play-by-play of Ronaldo’s tirade, published across 10 slides on an Instagram post.

In summary, Ronaldo left Portugal’s camp due to Jesus twice “breaking his word.” In the player’s account of events, the manager told him before this extended break that he’d play the first and fourth matches, also suggesting that his captain remained in Portugal while the team travelled to Norway and Denmark to leave him in the best physical condition.

This plan was rejected by Ronaldo, who was substituted without fuss in the win over Wales, and told on the day of the Norway match by Jesus that he’d play 30 minutes in Oslo. That cameo, however, never came to pass, sparking Ronaldo’s outburst.

The manager’s “absolute breach of trust”was complete when he went back on a decision to present an agreed version of events to the media ahead of the Denmark match, which he laid out in private alongside Al Nassr’s sporting ‌director Simão Coutinho. It was an eight-point document that outlined Jesus’ mistake in Oslo (making Ronaldo warm up but not bringing him on) and included the aforementioned comparison to Pelé and Diego Maradona.
“It was the second time he had broken his word to me,” Ronaldo wrote. “I decided ​to leave the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises.”

The 41-year-old admirably offered some respite from the self-indulgence by presenting several genuinely apologetic sequences to his teammates and the “Portuguese people”, admitting that he should never have left camp in the manner he did.
“The responsibility is exclusively mine,” Ronaldo noted.

Ronaldo is the most prolific goalscorer in international soccer. / Octavio Passos/Getty ImagesDespite an underwhelming World Cup that returned three goals and a premature elimination at the hands of eventual champions Spain, Ronaldo said he left the tournament with a “clear conscience” but wouldn’t rush into a decision regarding his future with the national team.
“It was my last World Cup, yes. But as for the rest, there’s time to think, to be with my family, and not say things in the heat of the moment,” the 41-year-old said.

He admitted in September that retirement was considered in the summer, but ultimately came to the conclusion that he’ll “finish when I feel like I'm not doing anything here [with the national team.” Ronaldo had thus committed to another cycle, potentially bowing out at Euro 2028.

The fallout with Jesus, whose appointment he described as the “right choice” upon his arrival, may bring forward his final international outing, even though Portugal’s captain has no plans to retire in the immediate aftermath.
“I can promise all my fans, naturally and especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches; there will be time for that,” Ronaldo wrote in his statement.

Portugal has made a perfect start to its Nations League campaign. / Octavio Passos/Getty ImagesAt the end of his statement, Ronaldo speculated about a potential suspension he may be subject to after storming out of camp, but said he “will be available” for Portugal if he is “physically well” and still scoring goals for Al Nassr in the Saudi Pro League. Jesus is open to reconciliation, too.

The merged September–October break concluded with Portugal winning all four of its games after goals from João Cancelo and Ronaldo’s replacement Gonçalo Ramos helped the Iberians come from behind to beat Norway on Matchday 4.

ftbpro_01m4at50k8s3.title: Barcelona, Real Madrid Learn Familiar Identity of El Clasico Referee
ftbpro_01m4at50k8s3.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Andrew Headspeath10:00 AM EDTAlejandro Hernández Hernández is reported to be the chosen referee for the Clásico. /  Jose Manuel Alvarez Rey/Getty ImagesThe first Clásico of the season is rearing up on the horizon, with Barcelona scheduled to host Real Madrid at Camp Nou on Oct. 25.
The meeting of Spain’s two giants will be the first since Barça confirmed the 2025–26 title with a 2–0 win over Madrid at Camp Nou back in May, and the first since José Mourinho’s return to La Liga.

Madrid will be desperate to make up ground in the title after going six points behind prior to the international break, while the presence of Mourinho adds extra spice to one of Europe’s most heated fixtures. The new manager has already raised the temperature in La Liga, bringing printouts of controversial refeerering decisions to the post-match press conference following the Madrid derby.
According to reports in Spain, the man in charge of keeping things under control in the Clásico will be referee Alejandro Hernández Hernández.

Speaking on Radio MARCA, journalist Roberto Gómez named Hernández as the man in the middle for the upcoming clash, though the official has not yet been confirmed by La Liga or Spain’s Technical Committee of Referees (CTA).

Responding to the news, the pro-Madrid MARCA host Raúl Varela responded: “Well that’s bad news ... I don’t like him as a referee, I don’t like his history in the Clásicos. I see it as absolutely unnecessary. I think it’s a wrong decision.”
Assuming Hernández does take the field on Oct. 25, what is his record as a referee and what does it mean for both teams?

Hernández was in charge of May’s meeting between the teams. / Pablo Rodriguez/Quality Sport Images/Getty ImagesHernández, 43, is no stranger to La Liga’s biggest fixture and has previously taken charge of six Clásicos—most recently officiating the last meeting between the teams at the end of 2025–26.
In the Clásicos Hernández has refereed, Real Madrid have won just once (back in 2015–16), while Barça have been victorious three times. The other two meetings have ended as draws.

The Canary Islander has only even given out two red cards previously, one for Sergi Roberto in a 2–2 draw at Camp Nou in 2023 and one for Sergio Ramos in 2017. He averages 3.3 yellow cards per Clásico.

In total, Hernández has refereed Barcelona 42 times, and La Blaugrana maintain a record of 26 wins, 12 draws, and only four defeats when he has officiated. He also taken charge of 37 Real Madrid games—21 wins, six draws, and ten losses.
Hernández was also selected as Spain’s sole referee at the 2026 World Cup and took charge of three group stage matches in North America.

No penalty was awarded for Aurélien Tchouaméni’s handball in 2025. / Pedro Salado/Getty ImagesThe most high-profile controversy of Hernández’s career came back in February, 2017 when he failed to award a goal in a match between Barcelona and Real Betis, when Jordi Alba’s shot crossed the line before defender Aissa Mandi was able to clear it.
Without the benefit of goal-line technology, Hernández waved play on—a decision the referee later publicly admitted was incorrect—with the match finishing 1–1.
"When the incident occurs, the match ends, and you see the replay, you're obviously devastated. I'd be lying if I said otherwise,” he told Movistar+.
Several years later in the frantic 4–3 Clásico of 2025, Hernández’s decision-making came under scrutiny from both sets of fans.

A Barcelona equalizer was allowed to stand despite a possible Frenkie de Jong handball in the buildup. Later in the game, the referee failed to award Barça a penalty for another handball by Aurélien Tchouaméni.

ftbpro_01m4awmd0wzs.title: Ronaldo’s Explosive Statement Inspires Withering Response From Portugal Boss
ftbpro_01m4awmd0wzs.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Grey Whitebloom8:30 AM EDTThe specter of Cristiano Ronaldo has hung over Jorge Jesus this fall. / Patricia de Melo Moreira/AFP/Getty ImagesCristiano Ronaldo used more than 1,700 words to explain why he had stepped away from the Portuguese national team in such spectacular fashion. The manager who inspired his hasty climb-down, Jorge Jesus, needed little more than a handful of words to offer his response.

Caught arriving at his home in Portugal by local broadcaster CMTV on Tuesday night, Jesus was quizzed about Ronaldo’s blockbuster statement. “I was in Leiria watching the U-21 national team match,” the head coach, who was not once mentioned by name in Ronaldo’s tirade, shrugged while leaning out of his car window. “Now I’m going to read Cristiano’s statement.”

The following morning, back in his car, Jesus had consumed the weighty tome. “I read the statement and now, like I do every day, I’m going to the federation headquarters to work, to think about the Portuguese national team,” he snapped. “I have nothing more to say.”

The 72-year-old is not one to wilt under the scrutiny of any player. Jesus took charge of the first of his 1,175 matches in management when Ronaldo was only 4. The subsequent decades have provided the tactician with thick enough skin to fend off even the most famous figure in his nation’s history. As Ronaldo explained in precise detail, this was not the first time this fall that Jesus had taken a dim view of his comments.

ftbpro_01m4ay54geyk.title: Real Madrid’s Winners, Losers From the International Break
ftbpro_01m4ay54geyk.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Andrew Headspeath3:00 PM EDTJude Bellingham was in superb form for England. / Carl Recine/Getty ImagesThe loooong international break of September–October 2026 is finally over and players are returning to club duty ahead of the domestic restart this weekend.
It’s back to the grind for Real Madrid stars whose focus turns towards grappling their way back into the title race after a disjointed start to the 2026–27 La Liga season.

Los Blancos have some catching up to do, and host Villarreal on Saturday. Whether the big break directly post-Madrid derby defeat was a good thing for Madrid’s players remains to be seen. Several have certainly relished the chance to play for their countries and José Mourinho will hope they can bring that positivity back to the Bernabéu. For others, well, it hasn’t gone quite so swimmingly.
Here are the winners and losers from the international break.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is winning over Thomas Tuchel. / Rob Newell/CameraSport/Getty ImagesThe right back has been in and out of the Madrid team and doesn’t appear to be fully trusted by Mourinho. However, he seems to be winning over England manager Thomas Tuchel (finally) and impressed with an assist to Anthony Gordon in the Three Lions’s 2–0 away win over Czechia.
He then shone again in the return fixture a week later—creating a match-high four chances.
36 - Jude Bellingham tonight makes his 36th England appearance while playing for Real Madrid, the joint most along with David Beckham.Royalty. pic.twitter.com/SxVCNpNiV3
Alexander-Arnold’s international teammate Bellingham continued his fine form with four assists and a goal in four matches for England.

Since the World Cup, the midfielder has looked like one of the planet’s very best once again, with former Manchester United midfielder turned analyst Roy Keane even boldly claiming that the 23-year-old could go on to become “one of the greatest players of all time.”

Marc Cucurella helped keep Spain’s run going. / Alberto Gardin/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty ImagesSpain extended its unbeaten run past the 40-game mark—a feat never before achieved in senior men’s international soccer. Cucurella played three out of four of La Roja’s wins, and was commended as “sensational” by manager Luis de la Fuente after the 4–1 victory over Croatia.

Eduardo Camavinga has Zinedine Zidane’s trust. /  Alex Gottschalk/DeFodi Images/Getty ImagesStuck on the fringes at Real Madrid, there was some talk of whether Camavinga might have been sold this summer. He stuck around but has yet to fully convince Mourinho of his worth as a starter.
However, with balance an issue for the manager in the early stages of the season, Camavinga showed what he can offer by impressing for France under former Madrid boss Zinedine Zidane.
In Les Bleus’ two matches against Belgium, Camavinga looked both assured on the ball and strong in the duel as his team ran out 1–0 and 4–1 winners.

Vinícius Jr. is out of form. / Shubhajit Roy Karmakar/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesNo player needed the international break more to blow off the cobwebs and boost morale than Vinícius Júnior, whose early season form has been the source of much concern. However, the Brazilian’s turgid start to 2026–27 only continued on national team duty, with the forward admitting he is struggling for confidence.
Vinícius Jr. did score a late penalty in a 4–2 win over Australia, but that was his only goal contribution in three games (Australia twice and India).
With Yan Diomande impressing for Côte d’Ivoire, Vinícius Jr.’s place on the Madrid left wing is coming under increasing scrutiny.
Mbappé’s lightning start to the season hit a bump after an injury scare on duty with France.

The Ballon d’Or nominee hobbled out of Les Bleus’s 1–0 victory over Türkiye after scoring the only goal of the game. His issue was subsequently diagnosed as a “hyperextended” knee, sparking fears he could miss a key part of Madrid’s season.
However, most reports suggest Mbappé should be fit to at least play some part in the clash with Villarreal. Whether Mourinho risks him is another matter.

Ibrahima Konaté did not play a minute of France’s games. / FRANCK FIFE /AFP/Getty ImagesAnother to be cursed by injury while on international duty, Konaté did not play a single minute of action for France but still returned to Valdebebas with a minor knee sprain.

ftbpro_01m4b1fp3zme.title: How Arteta’s ‘Doubled’ Arsenal Salary Compares to Rival Premier League Managers
ftbpro_01m4b1fp3zme.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Grey Whitebloom8:15 AM EDTMikel Arteta has been heartily rewarded. / Sebastian Frej/Getty ImagesArsenal have rewarded Mikel Arteta with a new contract until 2030 which is reportedly worth double what he was previously earning to make him the highest-paid manager in the Premier League.

“It’s a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal,” Arteta gushed once the worst-kept secret at the club had been finally confirmed on Wednesday.

“This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue. We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.”
Arteta is now thought to make more than £20 million ($26.4 million) per season over a contract which will stretch across the next four years, The Times report.

The managers in north London have to pay for accommodation somehow. / Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesFollowing the departure of Pep Guardiola, the Premier League’s previous top earner, Arteta is in a wage bracket all on his own. Arsenal’s manager also outstrips the big personality beasts of the international game, with the likes of Atlético Madrid’s Diego Simeone and Paris Saint-Germain’s back-to-back Champions League winner Luis Enrique the only ones who can come close to his earnings.

Intriguingly, the next highest-paid manager in the Premier League is thought to reside on the other side of north London. Tottenham Hotspur’s Roberto De Zerbi currently sits at the foot of the top-flight table, not that his pay packet would reflect such a position. Spurs were in dire straits when they went after the Italian tactician last spring, staring relegation in the face with the walking corpse of Igor Tudor stumbling around the dugout.

As the transfer window has proven, De Zerbi was able to guarantee a swollen influence over extravagant spending which has also found its way into his own pocket, with an annual salary of £12 million ($15.9 million), per ESPN.

Liverpool’s Andoni Iraola agreed a yearly package worth £10 million ($13.2 million) after leaving Bournemouth, the same outlet has reported. Enzo Maresca is thought to take home a similar sum at Manchester City but his arrival from Chelsea was costly enough.

After engaging in discussions with Guardiola’s former assistant before he ended up leaving Chelsea, City reportedly agreed to pay €20 million ($22.8 million) in compensation to smooth through negotiations.

ftbpro_01m4b3cak2hb.title: ‘Punished With a Ban’—Cristiano Ronaldo Facing Portugal Sanction Over Actions
ftbpro_01m4b3cak2hb.subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By James Cormack12:00 PM EDTCristiano Ronaldo is expected to be suspended by the Portuguese Football Federation. / Grzegorz Wajda/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesLet the record state that Cristiano Ronaldo’s abominable conclusion to his international career has not tarnished what he’s achieved with the Portuguese national team over the past 23 years.

The 41-year-old may be embarking on the most ungraceful of farewells, yet the abiding memories of Ronaldo’s story with Portugal, once he eventually decides to hang up his cleats, will remain wholeheartedly positive.

The record number of goals, however many ‘SIIUUUUUUUS,’ the World Cup hat-trick against Spain in 2018 and, of course, Euro 2016 glory. That’s what those who have displayed Ronaldo’s No. 7 jersey on their backs for the past two decades will cherish, not this bitter, childish fallout with Jorge Jesus.

And his story with the national team isn’t done yet. During an utterly remarkable near-2,000-word statement offering his explanation of events that culminated in his departure from the Portuguese camp on Sept. 30, Ronaldo said that retirement is still off the table and held himself accountable for his childish outburst.
He expects to be punished, but how could he be sanctioned by the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF)?

Ronaldo was furious with Jesus in Oslo. /  Cornelius Poppe/NTB/AFP/Getty ImagesRonaldo was undoubtedly apologetic to his teammates and the Portuguese people for acting how he did after Jesus twice "broke his word.”

“The consequence of this act of mine must be assessed and punished by the Portuguese Football Federation. I understand that the punishment should have no mitigating factors. I am not just any player; I am team captain, and that constitutes an aggravating factor,” he wrote.

Last November, FIFA regarded Ronaldo as above the law when it suspended the final two matches of his ban for a year, meaning he was available for the entirety of Portugal’s ultimately underwhelming World Cup campaign. Whether he ever serves the final two games of that suspension remains to be seen, and there’s no guarantee that he’ll be suspended by the FPF for storming out of camp.
Under the Federation’s disciplinary regulations, Ronaldo could be banned from anywhere between a month and six months, but only if his actions were deemed unjustified.

“Any player who, after being legally called up, leaves without justification or does not attend a training session, a match, or any activity of the national teams or related to the sporting representation of the Portuguese Football Federation or Portugal, shall be punished with a ban ranging between one and six months,” the regulations state. “In addition, if the player is a professional, a fine ranging between five and 10 accounting units.”
The financial penalty will be minor, but the strictest punishment would see Ronaldo miss the next two international windows and four Portugal matches.
Portugal is a two-time winner of the Nations League. / Lars Baron/Getty ImagesWhile Ronaldo himself seemingly wants to be punished, the FPF is unlikely to impose the most severe sanction.

The 41-year-old almost certainly won’t be available for the conclusion of Portugal’s UEFA Nations League group stage campaign next month, yet its record goalscorer could return for the quarterfinals next March.

“If I am physically well, playing for my club, with goals I hope, after serving the suspension that may be applied to me, I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team,” Ronaldo noted at the end of his statement.

Jesus’s side proved they can function rather well in the absence of their record goalscorer, securing back-to-back victories over Denmark and Norway after Ronaldo’s withdrawal from camp. The team also won against Norway days earlier when he was an unused substitute.

Still, so many of the players at Jesus’s disposal grew up idolizing their captain, and Ronaldo’s reintegration will likely be exclusively welcomed at some point next year. Even Jesus said he was open to reconciliation, although that was before Ronaldo’s statement.

Assuming Portugal wins its group, it will be paired against one of the four League A runners-up in the quarterfinals. Victory over two legs would secure a spot in the Finals, taking place next June. If Ronaldo is back in the fold, it could even be the final curtain on his entire career.
